@qed/glossary.entries.map.body.0: Levels are arranged in chapters. After the pen-and-paper exercises, each chapter adds a module to the same prover, retaining earlier capabilities as the course specifies. Passing a level unlocks those whose prerequisites are met; topics and challenges are optional branches.
@qed/glossary.entries.map.title: level map
@qed/glossary.entries.proofBoard.body.0: When a part requires a proposition, select one from the choices available in the level.
@qed/glossary.entries.proofBoard.body.1: Each level has tests: one uses the letter schema, while the others substitute everyday propositions. The circuit must pass each test. Tests expose mismatches; a general conclusion rests on the proof structure and its substitution rules, not on a few examples alone.

logic/glossary.entries.box.body.0: An assumption box expresses implication introduction. Select a temporary assumption A, derive B inside, and connect it to “Conclusion”; the box then yields \(A\to B\).
logic/glossary.entries.box.body.1: Click inside the box before placing a part, or drag a part into or out of it. The inside can use external premises and outer assumptions. A conclusion depending on this box’s assumption must discharge it through the appropriate rule before use outside. The arrow folds the box.
logic/glossary.entries.box.body.2: When the box yields A → B, its temporary is discharged. The conclusion no longer depends on it, but other premises and outer assumptions remain. The goal may not depend on undischarged temporary assumptions. Folding the box only changes its display.
logic/glossary.entries.box.title: Assumption box
logic/glossary.entries.circuit.body.0: Each part on the left represents an atomic proposition and outputs its truth value on the current row. The output “the sentence” receives the compound proposition’s value. Place and wire logic gates between them.
logic/glossary.entries.circuit.body.1: Select a row in the truth table to display the values of the parts on that row. “Run row by row” checks from the first row and stops at an error; “Step” checks one row at a time.
logic/glossary.entries.circuit.body.2: Some levels hide the target truth-value column. Others ask you to translate a natural-language statement into logical connectives and build its circuit.

qed/glossary.entries.assumption.body.0: A temporary assumption is a premise adopted for a derivation, not a claim that it is true in reality. If B is derived under A, an assumption box can discharge the dependence on A and yield \(A\to B\); other premises used by the proof remain.
qed/glossary.entries.assumption.title: assumption
qed/glossary.entries.automation.body.0: An automatic prover (a program such as E, Vampire or Z3) knows nothing of introduction or elimination and does one thing: negate what is to be proved, bring it with the hypotheses into , and look for a contradiction among the clauses. Isabelle’s sledgehammer hands them a goal, takes back the facts they used, and has metis prove it again in the kernel.
qed/glossary.entries.automation.body.1: Modern SAT solvers (DPLL, CDCL) look for a contradiction among clauses too, only far better at choosing: unit propagation first, and when stuck, a learned clause and a step back.
qed/glossary.entries.automation.title: automatic prover
qed/glossary.entries.axiom.body.0: An axiom is a sentence taken as a starting point without proof, a rule with no premises. K: \(A\to (B\to A)\); S: \((A\to (B\to C))\to ((A\to B)\to (A\to C))\). In this prover K and S can both be proved with assumption boxes, as lemmas; a prover with axioms alone can only take them as given.
qed/glossary.entries.axiom.title: axiom
qed/glossary.entries.backtracking.body.0: When a step can go several ways, keep every one, and when stuck go back to the latest place with another choice and take the next: this is backtracking. each tactic in Isabelle gives a run of results that the tactics after it try one by one; Prolog is the same proof assistant, where the order rules are written in and which subgoal is asked first decide whether the search stops.
qed/glossary.entries.backtracking.title: Backtracking
qed/glossary.entries.backward.body.0: Using rules backwards from the goal is backward reasoning: the goal is fitted to the rule’s conclusion (working out which sentences the rule’s ?A and ?B are; this step is called unification), and the goal is replaced by the rule’s premises, a new goal for each. A rule with no premises that fits finishes the goal. Proof assistants’ apply and rule use rules this way.
qed/glossary.entries.backward.title: backward reasoning
qed/glossary.entries.beta.body.0: (fun h => b) a works out to “b with h replaced by a”: β-reduction, calling a function. In a proof, a made and at once applied is a detour; β-reduction takes it out, proving the same sentence.
qed/glossary.entries.beta.title: β-reduction
qed/glossary.entries.bound.body.0: A variable covered by some is a bound variable. It is only a placeholder: \(\forall x.\, P(x)\) and \(\forall y.\, P(y)\) say the same thing, and renaming it changes nothing (α-equivalence).
qed/glossary.entries.bound.title: bound variable
qed/glossary.entries.capture.body.0: When an expression is put in for a variable, a free variable in it that lands under a quantifier of the same name is captured, and the meaning changes completely: putting y in for x in \(\forall x.\, \exists y.\, \text{Likes}(x,y)\) must not give \(\exists y.\, \text{Likes}(y,y)\). The cure is to rename the first: \(\exists y\) becomes \(\exists z\), then put y in, giving \(\exists z.\, \text{Likes}(y,z)\). Provers rename automatically when they substitute.
qed/glossary.entries.capture.title: variable capture
qed/glossary.entries.certificate.body.0: An outside prover is not in the kernel and may be wrong. So it need only hand over a certificate: which two clauses cancel into which, the steps traced back from \mark{bottom}. The kernel replays the certificate step by step, proving each with its own rules. Finding a proof is hard and checking one easy: the finder may be any program, and only the is trusted. Isabelle’s metis, and the tools in Lean and Coq that replay outside certificates, all work this way.
qed/glossary.entries.certificate.title: Certificates
qed/glossary.entries.classical.body.0: Adding double-negation elimination (from \(\lnot \lnot A\) infer A) to gives the corresponding classical logic. Together with negation introduction, it supports proof by contradiction and proves and Peirce’s law. Every classical propositional tautology is provable. Isabelle/HOL is classical; Lean can use classical principles.
qed/glossary.entries.classical.title: Classical logic
qed/glossary.entries.clause.body.0: Each string of “or” in the is a clause, and each item in it (a sentence or its negation) a literal. For a set of clauses to hold together, each clause needs at least one true literal. The empty clause has none and can never be true: it is \mark{bottom}.
qed/glossary.entries.clause.title: clause
qed/glossary.entries.cnf.body.0: First , then distribute “or” over “and” until every “or” is under the “and”s: strings of “or” joined by “and”, the conjunctive normal form. Each string of “or” is a clause. Distributing makes a sentence longer, exponentially at worst; automatic provers often use another conversion (naming parts with new letters) to avoid it.
qed/glossary.entries.cnf.title: conjunctive normal form
qed/glossary.entries.completeness.body.0: A system is complete for a semantics if every semantically valid proposition has a proof; this is the converse direction to . Every classical propositional has a proof, and classical first-order logic is complete for validity in all structures.
qed/glossary.entries.completeness.body.1: Completeness is not decidability: proof enumeration can eventually find a derivation when one exists, but may not stop otherwise. It does not contradict arithmetic incompleteness: the former concerns first-order validity across structures, while the latter concerns true statements about the natural numbers and arithmetic theories satisfying specific conditions.
qed/glossary.entries.completeness.title: completeness
qed/glossary.entries.connective.body.0: Connectives form compound propositions from smaller ones: \mark{not} (not), \mark{and} (and), \mark{or} (or), \mark{implies} (if … then …), and \mark{iff} (if and only if). In classical propositional logic, their truth values are determined by their components, so they can be represented by logic gates.
qed/glossary.entries.connective.body.1: Under classical truth-value semantics, these connectives can be expressed using “and” and “not”, or using “or” and “not”. The prover supplies corresponding introduction and elimination rules.
qed/glossary.entries.connective.title: connective
A proposition false on every row of a classical truth table is a contradiction, for example “\(\text{it rains}\land \lnot \text{it rains}\)”. The prover uses \mark{bottom} as a distinguished false proposition; a contradictory formula is not necessarily syntactically identical to \mark{bottom}.
In this prover, \(\lnot A\) is defined as \(A\to \bot\). To prove \(\lnot A\), one can assume A and derive \mark{bottom}.
qed/glossary.entries.contradiction.title: contradiction
qed/glossary.entries.contrapositive.body: The contrapositive of \(A\to B\) is \(\lnot B\to \lnot A\). From “if it rains, the ground is wet”, a dry ground rules out rain. The prover derives this direction using Apply and an assumption box.
\(A\to B\) alone does not generally imply its converse \(B\to A\) or its inverse \(\lnot A\to \lnot B\); both inferences have counterexamples.
qed/glossary.entries.counterexample.body: To show a proposition is not a , one truth assignment making it false suffices; this is a counterexample. One counterexample refutes validity, but failure to find one is not by itself a proof.
For a proposition with no premises, an assignment making it false rules out a premise-free proof in a sound system. When premises are present, a counterexample must also make every premise true.
qed/glossary.entries.countermodel.body.0: To show a conclusion does not follow, one is enough: the premises true and the conclusion false, a countermodel, the of first-order logic. Provers often come with a tool that searches small worlds for one, to check first whether the claim fails outright; Isabelle’s Nitpick is such a tool, and this game’s countermodel panel carries over its idea.
qed/glossary.entries.countermodel.title: countermodel
qed/glossary.entries.curry-howard.body.0: The Curry–Howard correspondence: a sentence is a type, and a proof of it is a program (a term) of that type. A proof of “\(A\to B\)” is a function, of “\(A\land B\)” a pair, of “\(A\lor B\)” a tagged value; \mark{bottom} is the empty type with no values, and “\(\lnot A\)” is “\(A\to \bot\)”; a proof of “\(\forall x\). …” is a function taking a thing, and a proof of “\(\exists x\). …” a thing paired with a proof about it.
qed/glossary.entries.curry-howard.body.1: The proof board’s rules match one for one: Apply is function application, the assumption box is λ, joining and splitting are making a pair and taking a component, and cases is branching on the tag. So checking a proof is checking a type.
qed/glossary.entries.curry-howard.body.2: Proof by contradiction has no program: none can conjure a proof of A out of “A cannot fail”. So intuitionistic logic is exactly the part programs can do, and classical logic must add proof by contradiction or excluded middle as an axiom.
qed/glossary.entries.curry-howard.title: Curry–Howard correspondence
qed/glossary.entries.currying.body.0: A function taking a pair and one taking its arguments one at a time can each be rewritten as the other: \(A\land B\to C\) and \(A\to (B\to C)\) give each other. Turning the first into the second is currying, named after Haskell Curry. In proof assistants functions of several arguments and rules of several premises are all written to take them one at a time.
qed/glossary.entries.currying.title: currying
qed/glossary.entries.decision.body.0: A program that, for every problem of a kind, stops and correctly answers yes or no is a decision procedure. Tautologies of propositional logic can be decided (work out the whole truth table); linear arithmetic and Presburger arithmetic have decision procedures too. First-order logic as a whole has none.
qed/glossary.entries.decision.title: decision procedure
qed/glossary.entries.declaration.body.0: In this game, a declaration specifies introduction rules for a new connective, from which the prover generates a corresponding elimination rule. This differs from an unfoldable and an assumed . The generated rule corresponds to the declared introductions; consistency also depends on the specific rules and system assumptions. Lean’s inductive types and Isabelle/HOL’s connectives have their own mechanisms; the game is a simplified model.
qed/glossary.entries.declaration.title: Declarations
qed/glossary.entries.deduction.body.0: The deduction theorem: if B follows from existing premises together with an additional A, then \(A\to B\) follows from the existing premises alone. It removes the dependence on A while retaining the other premises. In this game’s implicational fragment, the derivation can be rewritten using K, S and Apply.
qed/glossary.entries.deduction.title: deduction theorem
qed/glossary.entries.definition.body.0: A definition gives something already there a new name: a proof, a sentence, or a new kind of sentence. A definition can always be unfolded back into what it stands for, so adding one proves nothing that could not be proved before; an axiom is different, it states something new. Packing a proof into a part defines a lemma: in Lean, theorem chain := … is such a definition, and Isabelle too keeps each proved theorem under its name.
qed/glossary.entries.definition.title: definition
qed/glossary.entries.demorgan.body.0: \(\lnot (A\lor B)\) is equivalent to \(\lnot A\land \lnot B\), and \(\lnot (A\land B)\) to \(\lnot A\lor \lnot B\): a negation passing through “or” becomes “and”, and through “and” becomes “or”. Quantifiers too: \(\lnot \forall x.\, P(x)\) is equivalent to \(\exists x.\, \lnot P(x)\), and \(\lnot \exists x.\, P(x)\) to \(\forall x.\, \lnot P(x)\). Two of the directions, \(\lnot (A\land B)\to \lnot A\lor \lnot B\) and \mark{not}\mark{forall} \mark{implies} \mark{exists}\mark{not}, take proof by contradiction.
qed/glossary.entries.demorgan.title: De Morgan
qed/glossary.entries.dep-function.body.0: A proof of “\(\forall x.\, P(x)\)” is a function whose argument is not a proof but a thing: give it t and it gives back a proof of P(t). The type of the result varies with the argument, so it is a dependent function, its type written Π x, P x, in Lean simply \mark{forall} x, P x. \mark{exists} corresponds to the dependent pair (Σ type): a thing, and a proof that it fits.
qed/glossary.entries.dep-function.title: dependent function
qed/glossary.entries.dfs.body.0: Following one path to its end (done, or stuck) before going back for the next is depth-first search. It saves space, remembering only the current path; the price is that it may follow an endless path forever. So automatic tactics often bound the depth, or deepen it a level at a time.
qed/glossary.entries.dfs.title: depth-first search
qed/glossary.entries.diagonal.body.0: Lay out a table of x against y, look only at the diagonal of x against x, and flip every cell of it: what you get differs from every row of the table. This is the diagonal argument (Cantor, 1891). The barber, a set with more subsets than members, a machine rejecting its own code: each is the on a table.
qed/glossary.entries.diagonal.title: diagonal argument
qed/glossary.entries.dsyll.body.0: From \(A\lor B\) and \(\lnot A\), B: this is the disjunctive syllogism, the process of elimination. In the prover it is no rule of its own but a case split: the A side meets \(\lnot A\) in \mark{bottom}, which goes to ; the B side is the conclusion already.
qed/glossary.entries.dsyll.title: disjunctive syllogism
qed/glossary.entries.elim-rule.body.0: An elimination rule explains how to use a proposition with a : A follows from \(A\land B\); B follows from \(A\to B\) and A; and \(A\lor B\) supports reasoning by cases. Using a proposition in a proof does not consume it. Harmony requires elimination rules to correspond appropriately to the ways that connective is introduced.
qed/glossary.entries.elim-rule.title: elimination rule
qed/glossary.entries.equality.body.0: a = b says two names stand for one thing. It has two rules: everything equals itself (reflexivity); and when a = b, what holds of a holds of b (substitution). Symmetry and transitivity are proved from these two.
qed/glossary.entries.equality.body.1: Equations serve as rewrite rules too: the simplifier uses a = b to replace a with b in a sentence. By the chapter on proof terms, a = b is a type itself.
qed/glossary.entries.equality.title: Equality
qed/glossary.entries.equivalence.body.0: In classical propositional logic, A and B are semantically equivalent if they have the same truth value under every assignment. The biconditional \(A\leftrightarrow B\) states both implications and can be written \((A\to B)\land (B\to A)\).
qed/glossary.entries.equivalence.body.1: Equivalent sentences can stand in for each other: replace any part of a sentence with something equivalent and the whole keeps its truth. This is what the simplifier relies on to turn a sentence into another way of saying the same.
qed/glossary.entries.equivalence.title: equivalence
qed/glossary.entries.explosion.body.0: From a \mark{bottom} anything can be proved: the rule is often called the principle of explosion (Latin ex falso quodlibet). In the prover it is the part .
qed/glossary.entries.explosion.body.1: In classical truth-value semantics, a conditional with a false antecedent is true. The prover instead applies contradiction elimination to derive the desired conclusion from \mark{bottom}; this does not mean contradictory premises are true in reality.
qed/glossary.entries.explosion.title: principle of explosion
qed/glossary.entries.fol.body.0: A letter in propositional logic stands for a whole proposition. First-order logic also describes internal structure: names denote objects, predicates express properties or relations, and \mark{forall} and \mark{exists} mean “for all” and “there exists”.
qed/glossary.entries.fol.body.1: “First-order” means that quantifiers range over objects in the domain, not over predicates or properties. It can express “everyone is mortal”; quantifying over all properties requires a higher-order language.
qed/glossary.entries.fol.title: First-order logic
qed/glossary.entries.forward.body.0: Reasoning onwards from what is known is forward reasoning: a rule’s first premise fits a given, and its conclusion joins the givens. Unlike , it does not look at the goal. Some rules only go backwards (), some only forwards (): it depends on which side carries the bound variable when unifying.
qed/glossary.entries.forward.title: forward reasoning
qed/glossary.entries.free.body.0: A variable not bound by a relevant quantifier is free. The truth of P(x), for example, depends on a structure and an assignment to x. Treating the free variable as an unknown turns the formula into a query.
qed/glossary.entries.free.title: free variable
qed/glossary.entries.hilbert.body.0: A prover whose one rule is , all else being taken as an , is a Hilbert system: for the “if … then …” part of propositional logic, the axioms K and S are enough. Its proofs are hard to write, with no assumption box and every step assembled from axioms; the topic Without the box proves in such a system.
qed/glossary.entries.hilbert.title: Hilbert system
qed/glossary.entries.intro-rule.body.0: An introduction rule has a new in its conclusion: Join gets \(A\land B\) from A and B, Choose gets \(A\lor B\) from A, the assumption box gets \(A\to B\). To prove a sentence, its outermost connective says which introduction rule to use.
qed/glossary.entries.intro-rule.title: introduction rule
qed/glossary.entries.intuitionistic.body: Intuitionistic logic does not adopt double-negation elimination or as a general principle. It proves \(\lnot \lnot (A\lor \lnot A)\), but not excluded middle for arbitrary A without premises. For a premise-free disjunction theorem, the disjunction property ensures that at least one disjunct is provable; proofs from premises can also reason by cases.
qed/glossary.entries.isabelle.body.0: Isabelle (Paulson, from 1986) takes the LCF road: a theorem is an abstract type thm, and only a few functions in the kernel (one per rule of inference) can make one, with no proof term to keep. Its most used logic, HOL, is classical higher-order logic. Rules are written \mark{open-bracket}premises\mark{close-bracket} \mark{entails} conclusion, each in them filled in by unification, and tactics and the simplifier put rules together to use them automatically; sledgehammer calls on outside automatic provers.
qed/glossary.entries.isabelle.title: Isabelle
qed/glossary.entries.kernel.body.0: The kernel checks proofs against basic rules. Lemmas, tactics and simplifiers can help construct a proof, but their results must still be checked by the kernel.
qed/glossary.entries.kernel.body.1: A smaller kernel is easier to audit. Trust in a checked result still depends on the chosen axioms, the kernel implementation and its execution environment.
qed/glossary.entries.kernel.title: The kernel
qed/glossary.entries.lambda.body.0: fun h => b (also written λ h => b) makes a function: given an h, give b. This is λ-abstraction, as written in Church’s λ-calculus of the 1930s. The assumption box is λ: its assumption is the parameter h, its proof the body b, and outside comes a proof of \(A\to B\).
qed/glossary.entries.lambda.title: λ-abstraction
qed/glossary.entries.lcf.body.0: LCF (Milner, from 1972) set a design: a theorem is an abstract type only the kernel can make, and tactics are ordinary programs that make theorems only by calling the kernel’s rules. So however intricate a or clever the automation, none of it need be trusted, only the kernel. To write tactics Milner invented the language ML. Isabelle, HOL4 and HOL Light all descend from it.
qed/glossary.entries.lcf.title: LCF
qed/glossary.entries.lean.body.0: Lean (de Moura, from 2013) is built on dependent type theory. Every proof written ends up as a proof term, and the kernel checks that its type is the sentence to prove. The terms are kept, so anyone can recheck them with another checker: the de Bruijn criterion. Lean’s logic is intuitionistic at heart, classical reasoning coming from the axiom Classical.em; the mathematics library mathlib is written in it.
qed/glossary.entries.lean.title: Lean
qed/glossary.entries.lem.body.0: The law of excluded middle \(A\lor \lnot A\) states that A or its negation holds. It is a classical propositional tautology, but has no premise-free proof using this game’s intuitionistic rules alone. Adding double-negation elimination makes it provable; the result becomes <part-ref to="lemma:qed/lem"></part-ref>.
qed/glossary.entries.lem.body.1: <wiki-ref to="qed/classical"></wiki-ref> accepts excluded middle; <wiki-ref to="qed/intuitionistic"></wiki-ref> does not adopt it as a general principle.
qed/glossary.entries.lem.title: Excluded middle
qed/glossary.entries.lemma.body.0: A lemma is a proved result that can be reused in later proofs. For example, packages the inference from \(A\to B\) and \(B\to C\) to \(A\to C\). Its validity rests on its proof and permitted substitutions, not merely on test examples; unfolding it traces the proof back to the rules.
qed/glossary.entries.lemma.title: lemma
qed/glossary.entries.liar.body.0: “This sentence is false”: if it is true it is false, and if false, true. The island’s version is “I am a knave”, which nobody can say. It is no flaw of logic but a tool: let something speak of itself and say the opposite, and it proves that a thing cannot exist. Russell’s paradox, Cantor’s theorem and the halting problem are all of it.
qed/glossary.entries.liar.title: The liar
qed/glossary.entries.metavariable.body.0: A rule is written \mark{open-bracket}premises\mark{close-bracket} \mark{entails} conclusion, and the parts left open in it are metavariables: ?A and ?B any sentence, ?t any thing, ?P(x) any sentence about x. When a rule is used, unification fills them in. Isabelle writes every rule this way (in its metalogic Pure, \mark{entails} is “yields” and \mark{meta-all} “for any”); the holes ?m Lean’s apply leaves are metavariables too.
qed/glossary.entries.metavariable.title: metavariable
qed/glossary.entries.mgu.body.0: A solution of is a unifier. The most general unifier settles only what must be settled and leaves every other metavariable open; every other unifier can be had from it by substituting further. When first-order unification has a solution it has a most general one, unique up to renaming.
qed/glossary.entries.mgu.title: most general unifier
qed/glossary.entries.motive.body.0: In Lean, a = b is a type too. The only way to make one is rfl (a = a), and the only way to use one is Eq.rec, written h ▸ p: h proves a = b and p a sentence about a, giving that sentence with some of its a’s replaced by b. Which ones is said by a function fun x => …, the motive; Lean can usually read it off the sentence to prove. Symmetry and transitivity are built from these two: h ▸ rfl, k ▸ h.
qed/glossary.entries.motive.title: motive
qed/glossary.entries.natural.body.0: Natural deduction organizes reasoning by : introduction rules establish propositions with that connective, and elimination rules derive consequences from them. For example, \mark{and} has conjunction introduction and elimination, \mark{implies} has the assumption box and Apply, and \mark{bottom} has .
qed/glossary.entries.natural.body.1: Natural deduction organizes proofs using temporary assumptions and inference steps. Proof assistants can express rules in similar forms, though their kernels and rule systems differ.
qed/glossary.entries.natural.title: natural deduction
qed/glossary.entries.nnf.body.0: A sentence with no \mark{implies} or \mark{iff}, and every \mark{not} on a smallest sentence, is in negation normal form. Turn \(A\to B\) into \(\lnot A\lor B\), drop double negations, and push each \mark{not} all the way in with : every sentence comes to this shape, meaning the same.
qed/glossary.entries.nnf.title: negation normal form
qed/glossary.entries.normal-form.body.0: Take the detours (brought in, then at once used up) out of a proof term one by one until none is left, and what remains is the normal form. Every proof term of intuitionistic logic comes to a normal form, the same whichever detour goes first (strong normalisation and confluence). A normal proof uses only what appears in the sentence it proves, the starting point of Gentzen’s and Prawitz’s proof theory.
qed/glossary.entries.normal-form.title: normal form
qed/glossary.entries.pattern.body.0: A metavariable followed by variables (?P(x)) makes higher-order, which in general has more than one solution and is not even decidable. Miller found that when a metavariable is followed only by distinct bound variables (a higher-order pattern), there is one solution: ?P is the function with those variables as its parameters. Isabelle and Lean rely on pattern unification day to day; what is not a pattern waits to be settled elsewhere.
qed/glossary.entries.pattern.title: higher-order pattern
qed/glossary.entries.predicate.body.0: A predicate says what one or more things are or how they relate: “… is human”, Human(x), takes one; “… is a parent of …”, Parent(x, y), takes two. A predicate filled with things makes a sentence: whether Human(h) is true depends on whether h is human in the world.
qed/glossary.entries.predicate.title: predicate
qed/glossary.entries.proof-state.body.0: The goals still open, each with what it has to work from, are the proof state. A proof starts with a single goal, every rule used changes the state, and when no goal is left it is done. In Isabelle a proof state is itself a theorem \mark{open-bracket}subgoals\mark{close-bracket} \mark{entails} goal, one premise fewer for each subgoal proved; in Lean it is a set of metavariables still to fill.
qed/glossary.entries.proof-state.title: proof state
qed/glossary.entries.proof-term.body.0: A proof written as an expression is its proof term: a given is a name, Apply is p q, the assumption box fun h => …, Join ⟨a, b⟩. By the , it is a program as well, whose type is the sentence it proves. A proof term kept can be checked again by anyone with another checker.
qed/glossary.entries.proof-term.title: proof term
qed/glossary.entries.proof.body.0: A proof is a finite derivation from premises, axioms and inference rules. Each step is an allowed starting point or follows from earlier steps by a rule; checking rule applicability depends on formula structure.
qed/glossary.entries.proof.body.1: A propositional truth table grows exponentially in the number of atoms. A formal proof can use general rules and variables to establish a family of cases; reasoning about infinite domains still requires appropriate quantifiers and rules.
qed/glossary.entries.proof.title: Proof
qed/glossary.entries.provers.body.0: A proof assistant is a program in which a person and the machine write proofs together, every step checked by the machine. Each has a small : only the kernel can declare a theorem proved, and however clever the automation around it, everything goes through the kernel, so it cannot make a false theorem.
qed/glossary.entries.provers.body.1: This game’s prover is built that way from its first part: a kernel of a few rules, and lemmas proved with them. It borrows only proof assistants’ way of building a kernel and its parts; its own parts and notation are fitted to the game.
qed/glossary.entries.provers.title: Proof assistants
qed/glossary.entries.quantifier.body.0: A quantifier says for how many things a sentence holds: \(\forall x.\, P(x)\) says every x has P, \(\exists x.\, P(x)\) that at least one does. x is a variable standing for “any one”, and the quantifier reaches over everything after it.
qed/glossary.entries.quantifier.body.1: In classical logic, \(\lnot \forall x.\, P(x)\) is equivalent to \(\exists x.\, \lnot P(x)\); the forward direction generally requires classical reasoning. Quantifier order matters too: \(\forall x.\, \exists y.\, \text{Likes}(x,y)\) does not imply \(\exists y.\, \forall x.\, \text{Likes}(x,y)\).
qed/glossary.entries.quantifier.title: quantifier
qed/glossary.entries.query.body.0: A sentence with a free variable left in is a query: the things of the world that make it true when put in are the answer. The core of SQL and Datalog is first-order logic like this: a table is a predicate, its rows the things it holds of.
qed/glossary.entries.query.title: query
qed/glossary.entries.recursor.body.0: When an inductive type is declared, Lean’s kernel checks its constructors (its s) and then makes its recursor, its : one case for each constructor, the constructor’s type with its conclusion put as any motive (?R here). And.rec, Or.rec and False.rec come of it so; Isabelle’s conjE and disjE have the same shape. A recursor also comes with a rule of computation: met with a constructor, it computes on (ι-reduction).
qed/glossary.entries.recursor.body.1: Why the elimination rule can only be so: a declaration says “these are the only ways”, and the elimination rule writes that as a rule. It gives no more (introduce, then eliminate, is a detour that can always be taken out: what the rule hands back is what was handed in), and no less (take apart and put together, and the sentence is back). Proof theory calls this the harmony of introduction and elimination. If elimination rules could simply be written, one could write Prior’s tonk: introduced as “or”, eliminated as “and”, proving anything at all.
qed/glossary.entries.recursor.title: recursor
qed/glossary.entries.reduction.body.0: If A can be solved with a solver for B, A reduces to B. If A is undecidable, so is B: otherwise B’s decision procedure, with the reduction, would decide A. This is how spreads from one problem to a whole chain of others.
qed/glossary.entries.reduction.title: reduction
qed/glossary.entries.reflection.body.0: Reflection keeps no certificate: write the sentences to decide as data, write a , prove once that it is right, and after that every problem needs only the kernel to run the program, the proof term being rfl. Lean’s decide and Coq’s ssreflect take this road. How fast depends on how the kernel computes, so some decision procedures (Lean’s omega, say) produce a proof for the kernel to check instead.
qed/glossary.entries.reflection.title: reflection
qed/glossary.entries.refutation.body.0: When a set of clauses is unsatisfiable, is sure to reach the empty clause from it: refutation completeness. It does not promise to prove every sentence directly, only to find the contradiction when denying it is one, which is just enough: to prove C, show \(\lnot C\) contradicts the hypotheses. When it stops without \mark{bottom}, the clauses can all hold at once.
qed/glossary.entries.refutation.title: refutation completeness
qed/glossary.entries.resolution.body.0: Take a literal A in one and \(\lnot A\) in another, cancel the pair and join what is left with “or”: that is resolution (Robinson, 1965). Only one pair goes at a time. When the clauses have variables, the pair undergoes first. Reaching the empty clause is reaching \mark{bottom}.
qed/glossary.entries.resolution.title: Resolve
qed/glossary.entries.rewrite.body.0: \(l\longmapsto r\) is a rewrite rule: a place in a sentence that fits the left side l is replaced by the right side r. It rests on l and r giving each other (equivalence), or on l = r. A rule may carry a condition, and the rewrite is right only once the condition is proved. A set of rules used to the end must make the sentence “simpler” each time, or it goes round in circles.
qed/glossary.entries.rewrite.title: rewrite rule
qed/glossary.entries.rule-arrow.body.0: Every rule in the game is written \mark{open-bracket}premises\mark{close-bracket} \mark{entails} conclusion, the way Isabelle writes it: \mark{open-bracket}it rains; it is windy\mark{close-bracket} \mark{entails} it rains \mark{and} it is windy says “\(\text{with proofs of it rains and it is windy},\text{you have a proof of it rains}\land \text{it is windy}\)”. In a rule, ?A and ?B stand for any sentence and ?R for any conclusion.
qed/glossary.entries.rule-arrow.body.1: The double arrow \mark{entails} and the single arrow \mark{implies} are not on one level. \mark{implies} is inside a sentence: \(A\to B\) is itself a sentence, which can be proved, assumed and wired into other parts. \mark{entails} is outside sentences and relates proofs: with these, you have that. The kernel joins them: the assumption box turns “assume A, prove B” into a sentence \(A\to B\), and Apply goes back, from \(A\to B\) and A to B. Isabelle keeps the two levels apart: \mark{entails} belongs to its meta-logic Pure, \mark{implies} to the logic HOL.
qed/glossary.entries.rule-arrow.body.2: Lean has one arrow. A way to make is written And.intro : a → b → a ∧ b: a rule is an implication, and the way to make is its proof (the Curry–Howard correspondence), so a rule is applied just as a sentence with \mark{implies} is. The two notations say one thing: \mark{open-bracket}A; B\mark{close-bracket} \mark{entails} C is \(A\to B\to C\).
qed/glossary.entries.rule-arrow.body.3: When writing a declaration in the game, only the outermost layer of \mark{entails} is written: an intro rule is “\mark{open-bracket}premise; premise\mark{close-bracket} \mark{entails} conclusion”, each premise a whole sentence; a premise that needs premises of its own says so inside its sentence, with \mark{implies} and \mark{forall}, as in \mark{open-bracket}\(\forall y.\, y\) below \(x\to y\) reachable\mark{close-bracket} \mark{entails} x reachable. So writing a declaration and writing a lemma take one format: one conclusion, a few intro rules, each a row of premises side by side, with whatever is complex kept inside the statements. Isabelle’s own way writes that inner layer as a rule too, \mark{open-bracket}\mark{meta-all}y. \mark{open-bracket}y below x\mark{close-bracket} \mark{entails} y reachable\mark{close-bracket} \mark{entails} x reachable, so that the kernel splits it into subgoals when the rule is used, with no for-any box and assumption box needed first to prove a sentence with \mark{implies}. The two can be turned into each other and say the same; the game takes the first so the rules a player writes have one format and read simply. The elimination rule made from them still follows Isabelle, its premises with premises and things of their own: the kernel writes it, not the player. Lean has one arrow and writes intro rules as a constructor’s arguments, nearer the game’s way.
qed/glossary.entries.rule-arrow.title: the rule arrow \mark{entails}
qed/glossary.entries.rule.body.0: An inference rule specifies how conclusions follow from premises. For example, Apply derives B from \(A\to B\) and A. Letters represent proposition schemata and can be consistently instantiated as the rule permits. On the proof board, inputs represent premises and the output represents the conclusion.
qed/glossary.entries.rule.title: rule of inference
qed/glossary.entries.satisfiable.body.0: A sentence (or several together) is satisfiable when it is true in at least one case; when it is true in none it is a , also called unsatisfiable. In propositional logic a case is a row of the ; in first-order logic it is a world.
qed/glossary.entries.satisfiable.body.1: In classical propositional logic, A is a tautology exactly when \(\lnot A\) is unsatisfiable. Refutation-based methods negate the goal and check whether a satisfying assignment remains.
qed/glossary.entries.satisfiable.title: satisfiability
qed/glossary.entries.scripts.body.0: Isabelle’s Isar (Wenzel, from 1999) writes proofs as text for people, a structured proof: have proves a sentence on the way, show the one wanted, assume, fix and obtain bring in an assumption, an arbitrary thing and a thing taken out, and proof … qed is a block. The method after each by does one small step, and the system checks every row. Lean writes much the same: have h : A := by …, show B, intro, obtain ⟨x, h⟩ := …, and calc for a chain of equations.
qed/glossary.entries.scripts.body.1: A script, a proof term and a proof circuit are one proof: each row a part, each block a box. Large formalisations (the four colour theorem, the Kepler conjecture, the libraries mathlib and the AFP) are written this way: people write the structure and the lemmas, automation fills in the small steps.
qed/glossary.entries.scripts.title: Structured proofs
qed/glossary.entries.simplifier.body.0: A simplifier takes a set of rules, each a , and replaces wherever one fits in a sentence, until none fits. Each rule is a proved equivalence or equation, so every step is accepted by the kernel. Isabelle’s and Lean’s simp are such programs, the automation used most every day.
qed/glossary.entries.simplifier.title: The simplifier
qed/glossary.entries.skolem.body.0: Clauses hold only “for all”. In \(\forall x.\, \exists y.\, P(x,y)\), y varies with x, so it is replaced by a new function sk(x): \(\forall x.\, P\)(x, sk(x)). This is Skolemisation. The result is not equivalent to the original, but it is satisfiable exactly when the original is, which is all a search for a contradiction needs.
qed/glossary.entries.skolem.title: Skolem function
qed/glossary.entries.soundness.body.0: A rule is sound if its conclusion is true whenever all its premises are true. To refute an inference, a counterexample must make all premises true and the conclusion false.
qed/glossary.entries.soundness.body.1: The corresponding completeness property says that every semantically valid conclusion has a formal proof. Both properties are relative to a particular system and semantics; completeness does not imply a terminating decision procedure.
qed/glossary.entries.soundness.title: soundness
qed/glossary.entries.tactic.body.0: A tactic is a program that turns a into new ones. It can only change it a rule at a time, so however intricate tactics get, what they prove goes through the kernel. Isabelle’s auto and Lean’s simp and omega are tactics.
qed/glossary.entries.tactic.body.1: Combinators put tactics together into bigger ones: one after another (THEN), or else (ORELSE), repeat (REPEAT), on every goal (ALLGOALS, Lean’s <;>), maybe (TRY).
qed/glossary.entries.tactic.title: Tactics
qed/glossary.entries.tautology.body.0: A proposition true on every row of its is a tautology, for example “\(\text{it rains}\to \text{it rains}\)” or “\(\text{it rains}\lor \lnot \text{it rains}\)”. Consistently substituting propositions for its atoms preserves validity.
qed/glossary.entries.tautology.body.1: A complete truth table decides whether a propositional formula is a tautology, but n atoms require 2ⁿ rows. A proof instead derives its conclusion using rules, without enumerating each row.
qed/glossary.entries.tautology.title: tautology
qed/glossary.entries.theorem.body.0: A theorem is a proposition proved without undischarged premises. An assumption box discharges one specified temporary assumption; the result is premise-free only when all other dependencies are discharged too. In a sound classical propositional system, theorems are instances; a corresponding complete system proves every tautology.
qed/glossary.entries.theorem.title: theorem
qed/glossary.entries.truth.body.0: A compound proposition is built from atoms and connectives such as “if … then …” and “and”. In classical propositional logic, its value is determined by the values of its atoms. A truth table lists every assignment and result: n distinct atoms give 2ⁿ assignments.
qed/glossary.entries.truth.body.1: The conditional \(X\to Y\) is false only when X is true and Y false. When its antecedent X is false, the conditional is true by definition. This connective is material implication; it does not assert that X causes Y.
qed/glossary.entries.truth.title: truth table
qed/glossary.entries.undecidable.body.0: When no decision procedure answers every problem of a kind correctly, the kind is undecidable. The halting problem was the first (Turing, 1936). First-order validity is undecidable too, only semi-decidable (Church and Turing, 1936): what follows, a methodical search always finds; on what does not, the search may never stop. So automation can help, but never do it all.
qed/glossary.entries.undecidable.title: undecidability
qed/glossary.entries.unification.body.0: Unification solves equations \(s\doteq t\): it finds what to put in for each so that both sides become the same. First-order unification is solved by a few rules (Martelli and Montanari’s form: decompose, delete, clash, swap, occurs check, eliminate). Robinson invented it in 1965 for resolution proofs; it became the heart of Prolog, type inference and proof assistants.
qed/glossary.entries.unification.title: Unification
qed/glossary.entries.unit.body.0: A clause with one literal (a unit clause) states a forced fact; with it makes another clause one literal shorter. Passing such facts along is unit propagation. For Horn clauses (at most one literal without \mark{not} each) it is enough, and fast; SAT solvers do it first at every step.
qed/glossary.entries.unit.title: unit propagation
qed/glossary.entries.vacuous.body.0: \(\forall x.\, P(x)\to Q(x)\) holds when nothing satisfies P, true without checking anything: a vacuous truth. “All his children are at school” holds for someone with no children; that is right in logic, but in a query it is often not what was meant, and “has children” must be added.
qed/glossary.entries.vacuous.title: vacuous truth
qed/glossary.entries.world.body.0: Whether a first-order sentence is true depends on the world (also called a structure or model): what things there are, which thing each name stands for, which things each predicate holds of. A row of propositional logic becomes a world here.
qed/glossary.entries.world.body.1: A sentence always holds only if it is true in every world; there are infinitely many, too many to check, so it takes a proof.
qed/glossary.entries.world.title: world
qed/level.always.after: Whether a proposition is a tautology depends only on its logical form: put other propositions in place of its atoms and the verdict stays the same.
qed/level.always.intro.0.t: “If X, then Y” is written \(X\to Y\); “X and Y” is true only when both X and Y are.
qed/level.always.intro.1.t: A proposition true on every row is a <wiki-ref to="qed/tautology"></wiki-ref>.
qed/level.always.tasks.always.brief: Which of these five propositions are true on every row? Mark each one.
qed/level.always.tasks.always.hint.0: If you are unsure, expand the truth table and check its rows.
qed/level.always.tasks.always.hint.1: One false row is enough to rule it out.
qed/level.always.tasks.always.hint.2: “If it rains and it is windy, then the ground is wet”: can it rain and be windy while the ground stays dry?
qed/level.always.title: Always true
qed/level.and.after: A sentence proved from no givens is a <wiki-ref to="qed/theorem"></wiki-ref>: a tautology of the truth tables, here proved.
qed/level.and.intro.0.t: In the prover, “\(\text{it rains}\land \text{it is windy}\)” means what the <part-ref to="part:qed/gAnd"></part-ref> gate of <level-ref to="qed/g-and"></level-ref> does: it rains, and it is windy.
qed/level.and.intro.1.t: <level-ref to="qed/decl-and"></level-ref> declared “and”, and the proof board gained two parts: <part-ref to="part:qed/andI"></part-ref>, its one introduction rule, and <part-ref to="part:qed/andE"></part-ref>, the elimination rule made from it, whose two outputs give the left and the right. Every connective has its introduction and elimination rules; a system of rules organised this way is called <wiki-ref to="qed/natural"></wiki-ref>.
qed/level.and.tasks.and-1.hint.0: Take it apart, then put it back together in the new order.
qed/level.and.tasks.and-2.hint.0: The proof you just made can move into a box whole: assume “\(\text{it rains}\land \text{it is windy}\)”.
qed/level.and.tasks.and-2.intro.0.t: This time nothing is given: “\(\text{it rains}\land \text{it is windy}\to \text{it is windy}\land \text{it rains}\)” always holds.
qed/level.and.title: Both of them
qed/level.assume.intro.0.t: How can we prove “if A, then B”? We can temporarily assume A and prove B under that condition. An <wiki-ref to="qed/assumption"></wiki-ref> is a starting point for reasoning; it does not assert that A already holds.
qed/level.assume.intro.1.t: The <part-ref to="part:qed/impI"></part-ref> represents this reasoning with a box. Choose A as the assumption on the part and it becomes available inside. Connect the B proved inside to “Conclusion”, and the box gives \(A\to B\) outside.
qed/level.assume.intro.2.t: Outside the box, the temporary assumption A is no longer a given. The conclusion says that if A holds, B follows; any other givens used in the proof still remain.
qed/level.assume.tasks.assume-1.hint.0: What follows the “if” in the goal?
qed/level.assume.tasks.assume-1.hint.1: From inside the box, the givens on the board are visible.
qed/level.assume.tasks.assume-2.hint.0: How many \mark{implies}s are in the goal?
A box can sit inside a box. The inner one sees the outer one’s assumption and the givens on the board.
qed/level.assume.title: An assumption
qed/level.au-adder.after: Formal verification in chip design checks circuits in this spirit.
qed/level.au-adder.intro.0.t: A circuit can be written as equivalences, one per output wire against its inputs: the sum bit is “exactly one input is 1”, the carry bit “both inputs are 1”. A property of the circuit is whatever follows from them.
qed/level.au-adder.tasks.au-adder.brief: Design a proof assistant that proves the goals that follow and reports failure on those that do not.
qed/level.au-adder.title: A half adder (Legacy)
qed/level.au-cert.after: Finding a proof is hard; checking one is easy.
qed/level.au-cert.intro.0.t: The saturator makes dozens of clauses, and \mark{bottom} needs only a few. Tracing \mark{bottom} back through where each clause came from gives a <wiki-ref to="qed/certificate"></wiki-ref>: which two cancel into which.
qed/level.au-cert.tasks.au-cert-1.brief: Design a proof assistant that reaches \mark{bottom} from “\(\text{the alarm rings}\to I\; \text{get up}\)”, “\(I\; \text{get up}\to I\; \text{drink coffee}\)” and “the alarm rings”, and look at the certificate in the result.
qed/level.au-cert.tasks.au-cert-1.hint.0: The proof assistant of <level-ref to="qed/au-sledge"></level-ref> will do.
qed/level.au-cert.tasks.au-cert-2.briefN: Replay the proof assistant’s certificate on the proof board.
qed/level.au-cert.tasks.au-cert-2.hint.0: Each clause in the certificate names the two it came from.
qed/level.au-cert.title: Certificates (Legacy)
qed/level.au-clauses.intro.0.t: The new card “Into clauses” takes a proof state whose goal is \mark{bottom} apart, one <wiki-ref to="qed/clause"></wiki-ref> for each string of “or”: from here on, the wire carries clauses, no longer proof states.
qed/level.au-clauses.tasks.au-clauses.br: Design a proof assistant that splits each goal into clauses: the negation of what is to be proved, with the hypotheses.
qed/level.au-clauses.tasks.au-clauses.hi: The steps of this chapter so far, one after another.
<level-ref to="qed/au-negate"></level-ref>, <level-ref to="qed/au-hyps"></level-ref>, <level-ref to="qed/au-skolem"></level-ref>, and last “Into clauses”.
qed/level.au-clauses.title: Into clauses (Legacy)
qed/level.au-horn.after: In a SAT solver this is called <wiki-ref to="qed/unit"></wiki-ref>.
qed/level.au-horn.intro.0.t: Each round the saturator cancels every pair, and most new clauses go unused. In these clauses each has at most one literal without \mark{not}: they are Horn clauses.
qed/level.au-horn.tasks.au-horn.brief: Design a proof assistant that reaches \mark{bottom} without making more clauses than each test allows.
qed/level.au-horn.tasks.au-horn.hint.0: Some clauses have a single literal from the start.
qed/level.au-horn.tasks.au-horn.hint.1: A one-literal clause is something already forced.
qed/level.au-horn.title: Only what is forced
qed/level.au-hyps.intro.0.t: The sentences to search now sit among the hypotheses, but the simplifier has only ever rewritten goals. With Where set to Hypotheses, Rewrite and Simp look through the first goal’s hypotheses from the top and change the first place that fits.
qed/level.au-hyps.tasks.au-hyps.brief: Design a proof assistant that brings every hypothesis of each goal to conjunctive normal form.
qed/level.au-hyps.tasks.au-hyps.hint.0: The rules of <level-ref to="qed/sp-cnf"></level-ref> cannot deal with \mark{iff}.
qed/level.au-hyps.tasks.au-hyps.hint.1: Put <part-ref to="lemma:qed/iff"></part-ref> at the front of those rules.
qed/level.au-hyps.title: Rewriting the hypotheses (Legacy)
qed/level.au-iff.intro.0.t: The simplifier has no rewrite rule for \mark{iff} yet, and in the islander puzzles \mark{iff} is just what joins an islander’s kind to his words.
qed/level.au-iff.tasks.au-iff-1.hint.0: Split the equivalence first, then deal with each direction.
qed/level.au-iff.tasks.au-iff-2.hint.0: \mark{iff} is the two directions of \mark{implies} joined by “and”.
qed/level.au-iff.tasks.au-iff-3.brief: Design a proof assistant that turns the \mark{iff} in each goal into two strings of “or”.
qed/level.au-iff.tasks.au-iff-3.hint.0: Each shape of <part-ref to="lemma:qed/iff"></part-ref> is a rewrite rule too.
qed/level.au-iff.title: Equivalence away (Legacy)
qed/level.au-machine.intro.0.t: <level-ref to="qed/q-ancestor"></level-ref> and <level-ref to="qed/s-carroll"></level-ref> were proved by hand; this time, hand them to the proof assistant.
qed/level.au-machine.tasks.au-machine.br: Design a proof assistant that proves the goals that follow and reports failure on those that do not.
qed/level.au-machine.title: Let the proof assistant prove it (Legacy)
qed/level.au-negate.intro.0.t: Auto applies rules one at a time and bogs down as goals grow. An <wiki-ref to="qed/automation"></wiki-ref> takes another road: to prove C, assume \(\lnot C\) and look for a contradiction among the hypotheses. Isabelle’s Sledgehammer hands goals to provers of this kind.
qed/level.au-negate.tasks.au-negate.brie: Design a proof assistant that turns each goal into \mark{bottom}, with the negation of what was to be proved among the hypotheses.
qed/level.au-negate.tasks.au-negate.hint: <part-ref to="part:qed/raa"></part-ref> turns C into \(\lnot \lnot C\), that is, \(\lnot C\to \bot\).
qed/level.au-negate.title: Proving it backwards (Legacy)
qed/level.au-onepair.intro.0.t: “Resolve” refuses when two pairs could cancel. “\(\text{It rains}\lor \text{it is windy}\)” and “\(\lnot \text{it rains}\lor \lnot \text{it is windy}\)” hold two: cancel both at once and nothing is left, as if a contradiction followed. Why not cancel both?
qed/level.au-onepair.tasks.au-onepair.br: Find a row of the truth table where “\(\text{it rains}\lor \text{it is windy}\)” and “\(\lnot \text{it rains}\lor \lnot \text{it is windy}\)” are both true.
qed/level.au-onepair.tasks.au-onepair.hi: Try the row with rain and no wind.
qed/level.au-onepair.title: One pair at a time
qed/level.au-refute.intro.0.t: The empty clause has no literal in it, nothing that could be true: it is the contradiction \mark{bottom}.
qed/level.au-refute.tasks.au-refute-1.hi: “It rains” is itself a clause of one literal.
qed/level.au-refute.tasks.au-refute-2.br: Now prove \mark{bottom} from “\(I\; \text{take the bus}\lor I\; \text{cycle}\)”, “\(\lnot I\; \text{take the bus}\lor I\; \text{arrive on time}\)”, “\(\lnot I\; \text{cycle}\lor I\; \text{arrive on time}\)” and “\(\lnot I\; \text{arrive on time}\)”.
qed/level.au-refute.tasks.au-refute-2.hi: Two copies of the same literal merge into one.
qed/level.au-refute.title: Down to the empty clause
qed/level.au-replay.after: In Isabelle, proofs found by Sledgehammer are likewise replayed in the kernel by metis.
qed/level.au-replay.intro.0.t: The new card “Replay” hands the certificate to the kernel: each clause used must really come out of a hypothesis, and each step must be proved by auto from the two it came from. If all pass, the goal the clauses came from is proved.
qed/level.au-replay.tasks.au-replay.brie: Design a proof assistant that proves every goal: the proof assistant finds a certificate, the kernel replays it.
qed/level.au-replay.tasks.au-replay.hint: Someone has to find the certificate before the kernel can have it.
qed/level.au-replay.title: Let the kernel replay it (Legacy)
qed/level.au-resolve.intro.0.t: Between clauses one rule is enough. One clause has “it rains”, the other “\mark{not}it rains”: rain or not, one of them still holds with that literal taken away.
qed/level.au-resolve.tasks.au-resolve.hi: On the rain side, take cases on the second.
qed/level.au-resolve.title: Resolve
qed/level.au-saturate.intro.0.t: In <level-ref to="qed/au-refute"></level-ref> you chose which pair to cancel at each step. A proof assistant does not choose: the new card “a round of resolution” cancels every pair that can be cancelled, once, adding each new clause along with the two it came from. When clauses have variables, a pair of literals is unified first, then cancelled: “\(\lnot x\; \text{is human}\lor x\; \text{is mortal}\)” and “Socrates is human”, with x unified to Socrates.
Design a proof assistant that reaches \mark{bottom} where it follows, and where it does not, resolves until no new clause appears.
After one round, the new clauses may still have pairs to cancel.
qed/level.au-saturate.title: The saturator
qed/level.au-skolem.after: Skolemising does not keep the hypotheses equivalent, only satisfiable together or not at all: they are equisatisfiable.
qed/level.au-skolem.intro.0.t: Clauses have only “for all”, no “there is”. An \mark{exists} in a hypothesis with no \mark{forall} outside it can be taken out as <part-ref to="part:qed/exE"></part-ref> does; one under a \mark{forall} cannot: “everyone has a parent”, and the parent depends on the person. The new card “Skolemise” replaces such an \mark{exists} with a <wiki-ref to="qed/skolem"></wiki-ref>, say sk1(x), the parent of x. It takes only an \mark{exists} in negation normal form.
qed/level.au-skolem.tasks.au-skolem.brie: Design a proof assistant that brings each goal’s hypotheses to conjunctive normal form, then takes the \(\exists s\) out.
qed/level.au-skolem.tasks.au-skolem.hint: \mark{not}\mark{forall} must become \mark{exists}\mark{not} first, before the \mark{exists} shows.
In the second goal \(\exists y\) is under \(\forall x\): y depends on x.
qed/level.au-skolem.title: \mark{exists} becomes a function (Legacy)
qed/level.au-sledge.after: A \mark{bottom} reached by the proof assistant is vouched for by nothing but itself: the clauses were not proved by the kernel.
qed/level.au-sledge.tasks.au-sledge-1.br: Design a proof assistant that starts from the goal itself: where the goal follows, reach \mark{bottom}; where it does not, resolve until no new clause appears.
qed/level.au-sledge.tasks.au-sledge-1.hi: This chapter has already built two proof assistants.
qed/level.au-sledge.tasks.au-sledge-2.br: Find a row where the hypotheses all hold and the goal does not.
qed/level.au-sledge.tasks.au-sledge-2.hi: Look at the one-literal clauses after saturating.
qed/level.au-sledge.tasks.au-sledge-2.in: On the last goal, the proof assistant saturated without reaching \mark{bottom}.
qed/level.au-sledge.title: Hand it to the prover (Legacy)
qed/level.au-wrong.after: Outside provers fall within the <wiki-ref to="qed/lcf"></wiki-ref> design too: only the kernel need be trusted.
qed/level.au-wrong.intro.0.t: Someone hands over a prover said to be far faster than the saturator: it cancels every opposite pair two clauses share, all at once. It is on the board already, and it reaches \mark{bottom} on every goal.
qed/level.au-wrong.tasks.au-wrong-1.brie: Design a proof assistant that hands the certificate of someone else’s prover to the kernel to replay.
qed/level.au-wrong.tasks.au-wrong-1.hint: The other prover stands in only for the step that finds the certificate.
qed/level.au-wrong.tasks.au-wrong-2.brie: Find a row showing the first goal really does not follow: the hypotheses hold, the goal does not.
qed/level.au-wrong.tasks.au-wrong-2.intr: The kernel would not take the first goal’s certificate.
qed/level.au-wrong.title: The prover is wrong (Legacy)
qed/level.bot.after: Once the givens contradict each other, everything can be proved, and true can no longer be told from false.
qed/level.bot.intro.0.t: A witness says “the door is locked”, then “the door is not locked”. Both cannot be true.
qed/level.bot.intro.1.t: You met a in : a sentence false on every row. Here we write falsity as \mark{bottom}.
qed/level.bot.intro.2.t: <part-ref to="part:qed/botE"></part-ref> is the elimination rule of \mark{bottom}: from \mark{bottom} it proves whichever sentence is chosen on the part. This is <wiki-ref to="qed/explosion"></wiki-ref>.
qed/level.bot.tasks.bot-1.hint.0: “\mark{not}the door is locked” is “the door is locked \mark{implies} \mark{bottom}”: wire it into Apply’s “\(A\to B\)” input and “the door is locked” into its “A” input, and you get \mark{bottom}.
qed/level.bot.tasks.bot-1.hint.1: Once you have \mark{bottom}, use <part-ref to="part:qed/botE"></part-ref> and choose “the moon is made of cheese” on its part.
qed/level.bot.tasks.bot-2.hint.0: The goal is an “if … then …”: assume “it rains”. Inside the box it clashes with the given and gives \mark{bottom}.
qed/level.bot.tasks.bot-2.intro.0.t: In a truth table, an “if … then …” is true whenever its “if” part is false. Here the rules prove one instance of it.
qed/level.bot.title: contradiction
qed/level.box.intro.0.t: On a Saturday, if it rains I rest at home. It is raining.
qed/level.box.tasks.box.hint.0: What follows the “if” in the goal?
qed/level.box.tasks.box.hint.1: Click the empty space inside the box first, and the parts you place next land in it.
qed/level.box.title: Assume, then apply
qed/level.byContra.intro.0.t: “Suppose the door is not locked; that leads to a contradiction; so it is locked.” This is proof by contradiction.
qed/level.byContra.tasks.byContra.hint.0: The goal, “the door is locked”, has no \mark{not} in it. First think how to get “\mark{not}\mark{not}the door is locked”.
qed/level.byContra.tasks.byContra.hint.1: Use a box as in <level-ref to="qed/notI"></level-ref>, only this time assume “\mark{not}the door is locked”.
qed/level.byContra.title: Proof by contradiction
qed/level.c-arrow.intro.0.t: “If it rains, the ground is wet” and “it does not rain, or the ground is wet” say the same: each is false only on the row where it rains and the ground is dry.
qed/level.c-arrow.tasks.c-arrow-1.hint.0: The given does not say whether it rains.
qed/level.c-arrow.tasks.c-arrow-2.hint.0: Assume “it rains” first, then take cases on the given.
qed/level.c-arrow.tasks.c-arrow-2.hint.1: The “\mark{not}it rains” case contradicts the assumption, and a contradiction gives anything.
qed/level.c-arrow.title: Arrow away
qed/level.c-contra.intro.0.t: <level-ref to="qed/mt"></level-ref> derived a sentence’s <wiki-ref to="qed/contrapositive"></wiki-ref> from it. This time the other way: from the contrapositive back to the sentence.
qed/level.c-contra.tasks.c-contra.hint.0: Assume “it rains” first; what remains is “the ground is wet”, with no \mark{not} in it.
qed/level.c-contra.tasks.c-contra.hint.1: “The ground is wet” comes the way it did in <level-ref to="qed/byContra"></level-ref>.
qed/level.c-contra.title: The contrapositive, backwards
qed/level.c-dist.intro.0.t: “It rains, or it is windy and wet” and “it rains or is windy, and it rains or is wet” say the same: “or” distributes over “and”, as multiplication does over addition. With the “and” on the right and on the left, that makes two pairs, four directions.
qed/level.c-dist.tasks.c-dist-2.hint.1: Take cases on the two “or”s in turn. Only when neither gives “it rains” is “\(\text{it is windy}\land \text{the ground is wet}\)” needed.
qed/level.c-dist.tasks.c-dist-3.hint.0: As in the first task, left and right swapped.
qed/level.c-dist.tasks.c-dist-4.hint.0: As in the second task, left and right swapped.
qed/level.c-dist.title: Distribute
qed/level.c-dneg.intro.0.t: Two sentences that each give the other say the same thing: they are in <wiki-ref to="qed/equivalence"></wiki-ref>. “\mark{not}\mark{not}it rains” and “it rains” are such a pair.
qed/level.c-dneg.intro.1.t: Once both directions are proved, they make one part that switches between the two.
qed/level.c-dneg.tasks.c-dneg-1.hint.0: One rule you hold takes exactly two \(\lnot s\) off.
qed/level.c-dneg.title: Double negation
qed/level.c-either.intro.0.t: If it rains I take the bus; if not, I cycle. I do not know whether it will rain, but it will be one or the other.
qed/level.c-either.tasks.c-either.hint.0: Rain or no rain: take both sides.
qed/level.c-either.tasks.c-either.hint.1: When taking cases, both sides must prove the same sentence.
qed/level.c-either.title: One way or the other
qed/level.c-wall.intro.0.t: These five sentences are true on every row of their truth tables. How many does <part-ref to="lemma:qed/auto"></part-ref> prove?
qed/level.c-wall.intro.1.t: A search that finds no proof does not show there is none: the method or the depth may fall short.
qed/level.c-wall.tasks.c-wall.brief: Design a proof assistant that proves the required test goals and reports failure for the designated failure cases.
qed/level.c-wall.tasks.c-wall.hint.0: Try each with the auto you have, and see which it cannot prove.
qed/level.c-wall.title: What auto cannot prove (Legacy)
qed/level.cases.intro.0.t: Either I take the bus or I cycle; which, you do not know. By bus I arrive on time; by bike I arrive on time too.
qed/level.cases.intro.1.t: From “\(I\; \text{take the bus}\lor I\; \text{cycle}\)” alone you cannot take out “I take the bus”: perhaps I cycled.
qed/level.cases.intro.2.t: The elimination rule made for “or” goes case by case: one case for each introduction rule. is like an assumption box, but with two boxes: case one assumes the left, case two the right; when both prove the same sentence, it gives that sentence.
qed/level.cases.tasks.cases.hint.0: Place a Case analysis and wire the given “\(I\; \text{take the bus}\lor I\; \text{cycle}\)” into the input marked “\(A\lor B\)” on its part. The lower half of the part holds two boxes: case one’s “Assume” is “I take the bus”, case two’s “I cycle”.
qed/level.cases.tasks.cases.hint.1: In case one’s box put an Apply: “\(I\; \text{take the bus}\to I\; \text{arrive on time}\)” into its “\(A\to B\)” input, the box’s “Assume” at its top left into its “A” input, and the result into “Conclusion” at the box’s top right. Do the same in case two.
qed/level.cases.tasks.cases.hint.2: Once both boxes prove “I arrive on time”, the output at the Case analysis part’s top right gives “I arrive on time”: wire it to the goal.
qed/level.cases.title: Case by case
qed/level.chain.after: A proved result kept for reuse is a <wiki-ref to="qed/lemma"></wiki-ref>. Such a part is only a name for a proof, a <wiki-ref to="qed/definition"></wiki-ref>, and adds nothing to what can be proved.
qed/level.chain.intro.0.t: A proof, once wired, can be kept as a part and used from then on without opening a box. First, a part for each of a few moves that come up all the time.
qed/level.chain.intro.1.t: If it rains, the ground is wet; if the ground is wet, the road is slippery. So if it rains, the road is slippery. One step by instinct, but the kernel has no such rule.
qed/level.chain.tasks.chain.hint.0: The goal is “if it rains, then …”.
qed/level.chain.title: Join them
qed/level.contra.intro.0.t: “If it rains, the ground is wet”, so “if the ground is not wet, it did not rain”. This is the <wiki-ref to="qed/contrapositive"></wiki-ref>, and unlike the bad reasoning of <level-ref to="qed/onerow"></level-ref> it always holds: “\((\text{it rains}\to \text{the ground is wet})\to (\lnot \text{the ground is wet}\to \lnot \text{it rains})\)”.
qed/level.contra.tasks.contra.hint.0: Two \mark{implies}s, two boxes, one inside the other.
qed/level.contra.tasks.contra.hint.1: The inner box sees “\(\text{it rains}\to \text{the ground is wet}\)” and “\mark{not}the ground is wet”, that is “wet \mark{implies} \mark{bottom}”.
qed/level.contra.title: contrapositive
qed/level.copy.intro.0.t: Every new atomic sentence doubles the rows in a truth table. The prover’s <wiki-ref to="qed/kernel"></wiki-ref> takes a different approach: start from the premises and derive the conclusion one step at a time.
qed/level.copy.intro.1.t: The givens on the left are the premises; the goal on the right is the proposition to prove. A wire carries a sentence already proved.
qed/level.copy.intro.2.t: The cases below put different sentences in place of the letters of one pattern; the last, the general form, is the letters themselves. One board must pass them all.
qed/level.copy.tasks.copy.hint.0: A given’s dot is on its right; the goal’s dot is on its left.
qed/level.copy.title: Copy
qed/level.curry.intro.0.t: “If it rains and it is windy, the ground is wet” and “if it rains, then if it is also windy, the ground is wet” say the same.
qed/level.curry.tasks.curry-1.hint.0: The goal has two “if … then …”s, one inside the other.
qed/level.curry.tasks.curry-1.hint.1: Two boxes assume “it rains” and “it is windy” in turn; inside, join the two assumptions into one \mark{and} and hand it to the given.
qed/level.curry.tasks.curry-2.hint.0: One box will do: assume “\(\text{today is Saturday}\land \text{it rains}\)”, split it, then Apply twice.
qed/level.curry.title: Two conditions, one condition
qed/level.decl-and.after: “And” was not in the kernel before; the declaration is what makes the kernel know it. You may have noticed the <wiki-ref to="qed/elim-rule"></wiki-ref> written under the rule table, generated from the introduction rules: the declaration lists all the ways to construct the statement, so using it means considering each of those ways. Lean takes this road of declaring: “and”, “or”, “there is” and equality each come into its kernel by a declaration (inductive), and their rules are generated from it; only “if … then …” is built into Lean’s kernel.
qed/level.decl-and.intro.0.t: So far the kernel knows only “if … then …” (\mark{implies}): the <part-ref to="part:qed/impI"></part-ref> proves it and <part-ref to="part:qed/mp"></part-ref> uses it, both built into the kernel. A kernel does not automatically know new symbols: in dependent type theory, a <wiki-ref to="qed/declaration"></wiki-ref> can specify how a new symbol is constructed and used. Now the kernel is to know a new connective, “and”: both statements hold.
qed/level.decl-and.intro.1.t: A rule is written “\mark{open-bracket}premises\mark{close-bracket} \mark{entails} conclusion”: if its premises hold, the conclusion follows. The <wiki-ref to="qed/rule-arrow"></wiki-ref> connects the premises and conclusion of a rule; \mark{implies} means “if … then …” within a statement.
qed/level.decl-and.intro.2.t: An <wiki-ref to="qed/intro-rule"></wiki-ref> says how to prove a statement with a connective, an <wiki-ref to="qed/elim-rule"></wiki-ref> how to use it. The assumption box is the introduction rule of “if … then …”, Apply its elimination rule. A declaration writes the introduction rules; the kernel makes the elimination rule.
qed/level.decl-and.intro.3.t: Each “Derivable from” row is an intro rule: when its premises all hold, the conclusion can be derived. Tap “Add a premise” and build its sentence in the window that opens; another row is another intro rule. Tap “Check” when it is written.
qed/level.decl-and.tasks.decl-and.brief: Requirement: “\(A\land B\)” may be introduced only when “A” and “B” are both proved. Write its declaration.
qed/level.decl-and.tasks.decl-and.hint.0: There is one introduction rule, and it needs both at once.
qed/level.decl-and.title: Declaring “and”
qed/level.decl-bot.after: The elimination rule of \mark{bottom} has no case to handle, so once \mark{bottom} is held, every goal is derivable: the principle of explosion. “Not” comes from contradiction too: \(\lnot A\) is defined as \(A\to \bot\), “if A held, it would lead to a contradiction”. So with A and \(\lnot A\) both as premises, Apply gives \mark{bottom}, and from it any statement follows.
qed/level.decl-bot.intro.0.t: A contradiction is a situation that cannot hold, such as “it rains” and “it does not rain” holding together. Once reasoning reaches a contradiction, the premises it rests on cannot all hold.
qed/level.decl-bot.intro.1.t: The kernel writes a contradiction as the statement \mark{bottom}. \mark{bottom} never holds, so its declaration has no introduction rule at all: no premises are enough to prove it. The board holds that declaration.
qed/level.decl-bot.tasks.decl-bot.brief: Requirement: \mark{bottom} never holds: no premises are enough to prove it. Following the declaration of \mark{bottom}, fill in whether each case’s conclusion is derivable.
qed/level.decl-bot.tasks.decl-bot.hint.0: \mark{bottom} has no introduction rule. Under which premises can it be introduced?
qed/level.decl-bot.tasks.decl-bot.hint.1: The elimination rule asks for each introduction rule to be considered in turn. With none, what is left to consider?
qed/level.decl-bot.title: Declaring \mark{bottom}
qed/level.decl-check.after: Test cases can show a declaration wrong; they cannot show it right.
qed/level.decl-check.intro.0.t: A test case checks whether a declaration captures the intended meaning. Each case describes a situation: the available premises, the goal, and whether the goal is expected to follow from those premises.
qed/level.decl-check.intro.1.t: A declaration specifies which derivations are allowed. When a test runs, the prover gives a result according to the declaration and compares it with the expectation. A mismatch shows that the declaration does not capture the intended meaning in that situation.
qed/level.decl-check.intro.2.t: In this level, first write a case that agrees with your own declaration, then find a case that disagrees with another declaration, and last check one declaration in two directions.
Requirement: “\(A\land B\)” may be introduced only when “A” and “B” are both proved. Find a situation where the expectation meets the requirement and the declaration’s result agrees with it.
Choose the premises and the conclusion first, then ask what the requirement says: should the conclusion be derivable?
The table holds your declaration from <level-ref to="qed/decl-and"></level-ref>. Find a situation in which its result agrees with your expectation, and enter it in the table.
Requirement: “\(A\land B\)” may be introduced only when “A” and “B” are both proved. Find a situation where the expectation meets the requirement but the declaration’s result disagrees with it.
Does this declaration ask for the same premises as the requirement?
The table now holds someone else’s declaration. Find a situation in which its result disagrees with your expectation, and enter it in the table.
From the introduction direction alone this declaration shows no fault: with “\(\text{it rains}\land \text{it is windy}\)”, “\(\text{it rains}\land \text{it is windy}\)” of course holds. But the extra rule gives the elimination rule one more case, which hands back nothing, so “\(\text{it rains}\land \text{it is windy}\)” alone no longer yields “it rains”. One harmless-looking extra intro rule may show its fault only in use, so both directions must be checked.
Requirement: “\(A\land B\)” may be introduced only when “A” and “B” are both proved. Complete case 2 to reveal this declaration’s fault from the use direction.
This declaration’s elimination rule has two cases. What does the second give back from “\(A\land B\)”?
By the requirement, what follows from “\(A\land B\)” alone?

A declaration is checked from two directions. The introduction direction takes the declared statement as the goal and checks under which premises it can be obtained; the use direction puts it among the premises and checks what follows from it. The intro rules decide the first direction; the elimination rule generated from them decides the second.

The declaration on the table has one intro rule too many: from “\(\text{it rains}\land \text{it is windy}\)”, introduce “\(\text{it rains}\land \text{it is windy}\)”. Case 1 is already written and checks the introduction direction: the result agrees with the expectation. In fact this declaration passes every case written from this direction.
qed/level.decl-check.title: Checking a declaration
qed/level.decl-eq.after: This introduction rule is reflexivity; the elimination rule of equality is substitution.
qed/level.decl-eq.intro.0.t: Are the Morning Star and the Evening Star one star? To say two things are equal, equality has to be declared first.
qed/level.decl-eq.tasks.decl-eq.brief: Requirement: everything equals itself; two different names cannot be proved equal from nothing. Write the declaration of equality.
qed/level.decl-eq.tasks.decl-eq.hint.0: What do the two sides of an “s = t” proved from nothing have in common?
qed/level.decl-eq.title: Declaring equality
qed/level.decl-ex.intro.0.t: “For all” needs no declaration: proved for any thing taken, it is proved for all, and the kernel can already do that. “There is” is different: “\(\exists y.\, y\) is human” needs some thing and a proof that it is human, such as “Socrates is human”.
qed/level.decl-ex.tasks.decl-ex-1.brief: Requirement: “\(\exists y.\, P(y)\)” may be introduced once some thing is proved to satisfy P. Write two test cases whose expectations meet the requirement and with which this declaration’s results both disagree.
qed/level.decl-ex.tasks.decl-ex-1.hint.0: Having taken a thing, which sentence about it does this declaration ask for?
qed/level.decl-ex.tasks.decl-ex-1.hint.1: Which sentence about that thing does this declaration’s elimination rule hand back? By the requirement, does the same follow from “\(\exists y.\, P(y)\)” alone?
The declaration on the board does not meet the requirement. Write a test case for each direction, introduction and use, to find its fault.
qed/level.decl-ex.tasks.decl-ex-2.brief: Requirement: “\(\exists y.\, P(y)\)” may be introduced once some thing is proved to satisfy P. Write the declaration of “\(\exists y.\, P(y)\)”.
qed/level.decl-ex.tasks.decl-ex-2.hint.0: The introduction rule needs two things: a thing, and a sentence about it.
qed/level.decl-ex.tasks.decl-ex-2.hint.1: Turn on “for any x” in row 1, then add the premise “P(x)”.
Each row now starts with a switch, “for any x”: turned on, the rule holds for any thing x taken, and its premises may mention x.
qed/level.decl-ex.title: Declaring “there is”
qed/level.decl-iff.intro.0.t: “If and only if” makes one sentence of the “if … then” both ways.
qed/level.decl-iff.tasks.decl-iff-1.brie: Requirement: “\(A\leftrightarrow B\)” may be introduced only when the “if … then” both ways are proved. Write two test cases whose expectations meet the requirement and with which this declaration’s results both disagree.
qed/level.decl-iff.tasks.decl-iff-1.hint: Does each of this declaration’s two introduction rules need one thing or two?
With “\(A\leftrightarrow B\)”, what follows from “B” by the requirement? What does each case of this declaration’s elimination rule hand back?
qed/level.decl-iff.tasks.decl-iff-1.intr: The declaration of “if and only if” on the board does not meet the requirement. Write a test case for each direction, introduction and use, to find its fault.
qed/level.decl-iff.tasks.decl-iff-2.brie: Requirement: “\(A\leftrightarrow B\)” may be introduced only when the “if … then” both ways are proved. Write the declaration of “if and only if”.
qed/level.decl-iff.tasks.decl-iff-2.hint: Does the requirement need both at once, or is either enough?
qed/level.decl-iff.tasks.decl-iff-2.intr: A premise need not be a single letter; it can be a sentence with \mark{implies} in it, built with the connective in the premise window. A rule is written with one layer of \mark{entails}; whatever a premise needs in turn goes inside its sentence.
qed/level.decl-iff.title: Declaring “if and only if”
qed/level.decl-or.after: The elimination rule made from the intro rules of “or” is what is usually called reasoning by cases.
qed/level.decl-or.intro.0.t: It may be introduced when both are proved, too. The declaration of “or” on the board does not meet the requirement: first write test cases that find its fault, then write one yourself.
qed/level.decl-or.tasks.decl-or-1.brief: Requirement: “\(A\lor B\)” may be introduced once either “A” or “B” is proved. The conclusion is fixed to “A”. Write a test case whose expectation meets the requirement but with which this declaration’s result disagrees.
qed/level.decl-or.tasks.decl-or-1.hint.0: With “\(A\lor B\)” at hand, does the requirement let you conclude “A”?
qed/level.decl-or.tasks.decl-or-2.after: The elimination rule is made from the intro rules, so a case that tests the elimination rule can also find a fault in the intro rules.
qed/level.decl-or.tasks.decl-or-2.brief: Requirement: “\(A\lor B\)” may be introduced once either “A” or “B” is proved. The conclusion is fixed to “C”. Write a test case on which this declaration’s result disagrees with the expectation.
