qed/level.decl-or.tasks.decl-or-2.hint.0: The conclusion is not “or” itself, so “\(A\lor B\)” must be among the premises: the case tests its elimination rule. By the requirement, when does “C” not follow?
qed/level.decl-or.tasks.decl-or-3.brief: Requirement: “\(A\lor B\)” may be introduced once either “A” or “B” is proved. Write the declaration of “or” from an empty board, so that it meets the requirement.
qed/level.decl-or.tasks.decl-or-3.hint.0: The requirement has two separate situations, each needing one thing.
qed/level.decl-or.title: Declaring “or”
qed/level.decl-order.after: Test cases see only what can be derived, not how a rule is written; the kernel keeps to the rule written down.
qed/level.decl-order.intro.0.t: The “and” of <level-ref to="qed/decl-and"></level-ref> takes “it rains” first, then “it is windy”. Would the other order do? Can test cases tell?
qed/level.decl-order.intro.1.t: Declaration 1 takes “it rains” first, declaration 2 “it is windy” first. Write a case for each direction, introduction and use, expected derivable, and check both declarations.
Requirement: “\(A\land B\)” may be introduced only when “A” and “B” are both proved. Write two test cases whose expectations meet the requirement and with which this declaration’s results both agree.
Does the order of the premises change what introducing “and” needs?
qed/level.decl-order.tasks.decl-order.br: Requirement: “\(A\land B\)” may be introduced only when “A” and “B” are both proved. Write two test cases whose expectations meet the requirement and with which this declaration’s results both agree.
qed/level.decl-order.tasks.decl-order.hi: What does introducing “and” need? What can be taken out of an “and”?
qed/level.decl-order.title: The other order
qed/level.decl-strength.intro.0.t: A declaration can be wrong on either side: too strong, failing to introduce when it should; too weak, introducing when it should not. Both faults show from the introduction and the use direction alike.
qed/level.decl-strength.tasks.decl-stren: Requirement: “\(A\land B\)” may be introduced only when “A” and “B” are both proved. Write two test cases whose expectations meet the requirement and with which this declaration’s results both disagree.
What does “and” need, by the requirement? What does this declaration’s intro rule ask for?

The table holds someone else’s declaration of “and”. Its introduction conditions are too strong: premises that should be enough to prove an “and” statement are not enough under this declaration. Write a test case for each direction, introduction and use, to expose its fault.

Requirement: “\(A\land B\)” may be introduced only when “A” and “B” are both proved. Write two test cases whose expectations meet the requirement and with which this declaration’s results both disagree.
How much does each of this declaration’s intro rules need? How much does “and” need, by the requirement?
The table now holds another declaration of “and”. This time its introduction conditions are too weak: it accepts premises that should not be enough to prove an “and” statement.
A declaration determines both when “\(\text{it rains}\land \text{it is windy}\)” can be introduced and what follows from it. Again write a test case for each direction to expose the error.
qed/level.decl-strength.title: Too strong, too weak
qed/level.decl-three.intro.0.t: “And” and “or” each join two sentences. Here there are three.
Requirement: “\(A\land (B\land C)\)” may be introduced only when “A”, “B” and “C” are all proved. Write two test cases whose expectations meet the requirement and with which this declaration’s results both disagree.
How many introduction rules does this declaration have, and what does each need?
Into how many cases does the elimination rule made from it split, and what does each case hand back?
The declaration on the board does not meet the requirement. Write a test case for each direction, introduction and use, to find its fault.
The more introduction rules, the easier to introduce and the harder to use: each one more is one more case to handle when taking it apart.
Requirement: “\(A\lor (B\lor C)\)” may be introduced once any one of “A”, “B”, “C” is proved. Following this declaration, fill in whether each case’s conclusion is derivable.
To derive a sentence from “one of three”, each of the three cases must derive it on its own.
The board holds the declaration of “one of three”: three introduction rules, each needing one thing.
qed/level.decl-three.title: Three of them
qed/level.decl-true.after: True is often written \mark{top}, the very opposite of \mark{bottom}: knowing it holds tells you nothing more.
qed/level.decl-true.intro.0.t: The opposite of \mark{bottom}: True always holds. The table holds its declaration: one intro rule with no premises, needing nothing.
qed/level.decl-true.tasks.decl-true.brie: Requirement: True needs nothing: it may be introduced whatever is at hand, even with nothing at all. Following this declaration, fill in whether each case’s conclusion is derivable.
qed/level.decl-true.tasks.decl-true.hint: This declaration’s elimination rule has one case, which hands back nothing.
qed/level.decl-true.title: Declaring True
qed/level.decl-two.after: “Exactly one agrees” cannot be declared, though: an introduction rule can say what makes a sentence, never what stops it.
qed/level.decl-two.intro.0.t: What is declared need not be a connective: whatever holds in ways that can be spelled out can be declared.
qed/level.decl-two.intro.1.t: The declaration of “the motion passes” on the board does not meet the requirement. Write a test case for each direction, introduction and use, to find its fault.
qed/level.decl-two.tasks.decl-two.brief: Requirement: “the motion passes” may be introduced only when at least two of “A”, “B”, “C” are proved. Write two test cases whose expectations meet the requirement and with which this declaration’s results both disagree.
qed/level.decl-two.tasks.decl-two.hint.0: How many pairs can be taken from the three? Which does this declaration write out?
qed/level.decl-two.tasks.decl-two.hint.1: Which sentence is in every one of this declaration’s introduction rules?
qed/level.decl-two.title: At least two
qed/level.demorgan.intro.0.t: “Neither Saturday nor Sunday” and “not (Saturday or Sunday)” say the same; so do “not (Saturday and Sunday)” and “not Saturday, or not Sunday”. These are <wiki-ref to="qed/demorgan"></wiki-ref>.
qed/level.demorgan.tasks.demorgan-1.hint: Each half of the goal is a negation.
Assume “today is Saturday” and see how it contradicts the given.
qed/level.demorgan.tasks.demorgan-2.hint: Assume “\(\text{today is Saturday}\lor \text{today is Sunday}\)” and get a contradiction in each case.
qed/level.demorgan.tasks.demorgan-3.hint: The goal is again a negation.
Assume “\(\text{today is Saturday}\land \text{today is Sunday}\)”, then take cases on the given.
qed/level.demorgan.tasks.demorgan-4.hint: The given does not say which one fails.
Today is Saturday, or it is not: take both sides.
qed/level.demorgan.title: De Morgan
qed/level.dist.tasks.dist.hint.0: Split the \mark{and} first, then take cases on the “\(\text{it rains}\lor \text{it is windy}\)” it gives.
qed/level.dist.tasks.dist.hint.1: In each case, join “today is Saturday” with that case’s assumption, then put it on the matching side of the \mark{or}.
qed/level.dist.title: Distribute
qed/level.drinker.after: It sounds absurd, yet it is a theorem of classical logic: the proof says such a person exists without saying who.
qed/level.drinker.intro.0.t: There is at least one person in the pub. “\(\exists x.\, x\) is drinking \mark{implies} \(\forall y.\, y\) is drinking” says: there is someone such that, if they drink, everyone drinks.
qed/level.drinker.tasks.drinker.hint.0: Do not look for that person yet. Ask first: is everyone drinking?
qed/level.drinker.tasks.drinker.hint.1: If not everyone is drinking, what does <part-ref to="lemma:qed/dm"></part-ref> give?
qed/level.drinker.title: The drinker paradox
qed/level.dsyll.after: This is the <wiki-ref to="qed/dsyll"></wiki-ref>, the logic behind every process of elimination.
qed/level.dsyll.intro.0.t: Bus or bike; not the bus, so the bike.
qed/level.dsyll.tasks.dsyll.hint.0: Take cases. On the “I take the bus” side it runs into “\(\lnot I\; \text{take the bus}\)” and gives \mark{bottom}; from a contradiction, anything.
qed/level.dsyll.title: Rule one out, the other remains
qed/level.e-count.after: Only one row lights up: a is a knight, b and c are knaves. “At least one” is a string of “or”s; “at most one” is an “or” for every pair, joined by “and”; “not the only one” is a string of “or”s too. Problems such as rostering (at least so many on duty, at most so many on leave at once, someone who may not work alone) are put to a SAT solver the same way: each counting phrase rewritten as strings of “or”s, joined together.
qed/level.e-count.intro.0.t: “At least”, “at most” and “only” speak of how many, and and, or and not have no gate that counts. Such words must first be said another way, as a sentence about whether each person is a knight.
qed/level.e-count.tasks.e-count.brief: a says: “At least one of the three of us is a knave.” b says: “At most one of the three of us is a knave.” c says: “a is not the only knight.” Translate what the three say into logic and wire it: the board outputs true on exactly the rows where what each says fits what they are.
qed/level.e-count.tasks.e-count.hint.0: “At least one is a knave”: of the three, who might that knave be?
qed/level.e-count.tasks.e-count.hint.1: “At most one knave” means no two people are knaves at once. Pick any two people: what must be true of them?
qed/level.e-count.tasks.e-count.hint.2: “a is not the only knight”: either a is not a knight, or there is another knight.
qed/level.e-count.title: At least and at most
qed/level.e-one.tasks.e-one.brief: a says: “At least one of us two is a knave.” Translate this into logic and wire it: the board outputs true on exactly the rows where what a says fits what a is.
qed/level.e-one.tasks.e-one.hint.0: Translate what a says first, then “a says”.
qed/level.e-one.tasks.e-one.hint.1: “a is a knave” is “a is not a knight”.
qed/level.e-one.title: One islander speaks
qed/level.e-says.after: Both could be knights, or both could be knaves. This clue leaves two possibilities. In the next puzzles, you’ll use the same method to check more complicated statements.
qed/level.e-says.intro.0.t: You arrive on an island and meet two residents, a and b. Every islander is either a knight, who always tells the truth, or a knave, who always lies.
qed/level.e-says.intro.1.t: a speaks first. Put “a is a knight” and what a says into one formula, then use the truth table to find the identities that fit the island’s rules.
Use the cards to express how a’s identity must relate to this clue.
If a is a knight, the statement must be true. What if a is a knave?
Which connective requires both sides to have the same truth value?
qed/level.e-says.tasks.e-says.brief: Wire your formula and run the truth table. Find the rows where a’s statement fits a’s identity.
qed/level.e-says.tasks.e-says.hint.0: Use the two knight-status inputs for the two propositions in your formula, then connect them with the corresponding gate.
qed/level.e-says.title: Knights and Knaves: The First Clue
qed/level.e-three.after: Finding a row on which several sentences are all true is the <wiki-ref to="qed/satisfiable"></wiki-ref> problem (SAT).
qed/level.e-three.intro.0.t: Three people, and the table has eight rows.
qed/level.e-three.tasks.e-three.brief: a says: “b is a knave.” b says: “c is a knave.” c says: “a and b are both knaves.” Translate what the three say into logic and wire it: the board outputs true on exactly the rows where what each says fits what they are.
qed/level.e-three.tasks.e-three.hint.0: In what c says, which part does the negation cover?
qed/level.e-three.tasks.e-three.hint.1: Translate each person’s words on their own; all three must hold at once.
qed/level.e-three.title: Three islanders speak
qed/level.e-two.tasks.e-two.brief: a says: “b is a knave.” b says: “We are both knights.” Translate what both say into logic and wire it: the board outputs true on exactly the rows where what each says fits what they are.
qed/level.e-two.tasks.e-two.hint.0: Translate what each person says on its own.
qed/level.e-two.title: Two islanders speak
qed/level.e-words.after: All four rows are false. The rule says rain makes the ground wet, so it can’t hold alongside a report of rain leaving the ground dry. A formula that is false on every row is a <wiki-ref to="qed/contradiction"></wiki-ref>.
qed/level.e-words.intro.0.t: You can wire a simple sentence directly. With a longer sentence, it’s easy to lose track of what each gate should connect. Translate the sentence into a logical formula first, then use the formula to guide your wiring.
qed/level.e-words.intro.1.t: Practice translating a short sentence, then try a more complicated rain report. In the circuit, use the basic claims as inputs and turn the connectives into gates. The truth table runs the circuit once for each combination of inputs.
qed/level.e-words.tasks.e-words-translat: The log gives a general rule and describes what just happened. Translate the two claims separately, then use the cards to build one formula that says both hold.
Start with “Whenever it rains, the ground in the yard gets wet”. Which connective expresses that condition?
The second sentence says it rained and the ground stayed dry. Join the two sentences with another And.
The caretaker wrote in the log: “Whenever it rains, the ground in the yard gets wet. It rained just now, but the ground was still dry.”
qed/level.e-words.tasks.e-words-warmup.b: Start with a short sentence. Find its two claims and use the cards to put them into one formula.
qed/level.e-words.tasks.e-words-warmup.h: The sentence says both that it’s raining and that the ground is wet. Which connective requires both claims to be true?
qed/level.e-words.tasks.e-words-warmup.s: Rain is still falling on the wet courtyard.
qed/level.e-words.tasks.g-always-2.brief: Wire the formula you just built. Run the truth table and see whether any row makes both claims in the report true.
Revisit Translate the report to check your formula. Wire the inner connectives first, then feed their outputs into the outer ones.
qed/level.e-words.title: Does the rain report add up?
qed/level.fo-all.after: A sentence that always holds is true in every world, and there are infinitely many worlds, of any size.
qed/level.fo-all.intro.0.t: The universal \mark{forall} reads “for all”: \(\forall x.\, P(x)\) says every thing x in the world satisfies P.
qed/level.fo-all.intro.1.t: First build a sentence as a formula; when it is wrong, the checker may show a small world where it and the target differ. Then someone else has translated the sentence too, and it is your turn to show with a world that they got it wrong.
qed/level.fo-all.tasks.fo-all-1.brief: Use the cards to build a formula for this sentence.
qed/level.fo-all.tasks.fo-all-1.hint.0: “Every human is mortal”: for every thing x, if x is human then x is mortal.
qed/level.fo-all.tasks.fo-all-1.hint.1: Writing “\(x\; \text{is human}\land x\; \text{is mortal}\)” says every thing in the world is human.
qed/level.fo-all.tasks.fo-all-2.brief: You built this sentence as a formula; this is someone else’s. Build a world where the two differ in truth.
qed/level.fo-all.tasks.fo-all-2.hint.0: Tap a thing to make it human; tap again to undo.
qed/level.fo-all.tasks.fo-all-2.hint.1: What does this translation say of every thing? What if the world holds a thing that is not human?
In propositional logic, whether a sentence is true depends on the row of the truth table. In first-order logic it depends on the <wiki-ref to="qed/world"></wiki-ref>: how many things there are, what each is and how they relate.
Above are your translation and someone else’s. To show theirs is wrong, build a world where the two differ: choose below how many things there are, then tap what holds of each. A run marks above whether each translation is true in this world.
qed/level.fo-all.tasks.fo-all-3.brief: You built this sentence as a formula; this is someone else’s. Build a world where the two differ in truth.
qed/level.fo-all.tasks.fo-all-3.hint.0: A human who is not mortal.
qed/level.fo-all.title: For all \mark{forall}
qed/level.fo-atoms.brief: Use the cards to build a formula for this sentence.
qed/level.fo-atoms.intro.0.t: In propositional logic a letter stands for a whole sentence: saying whether each person is mortal takes a letter per person, and “everyone” or “someone” cannot be said at all.
qed/level.fo-atoms.intro.1.t: takes sentences apart: a name stands for a thing, and a says what a thing is or how things relate. “Socrates is human” is written Human(h), “Ann likes Bo” Likes(i, j): the order of the places matters.
qed/level.fo-atoms.intro.2.t: To translate a sentence, find its frame first: the connectives often hide in the wording, “yet” is “and”, “either … or …” is “or”, “only if” is “if … then …” with the condition at the end. No proofs in this chapter yet: first how to say a sentence, and how to tell whether it is true in a world.
qed/level.fo-atoms.tasks.fo-atoms-1.hint: “Yet”, “but” and “and” are all \mark{and} in logic: both halves hold.
In “\mark{circle-1} is a parent of \mark{circle-2}”, who is \mark{circle-1}, who is \mark{circle-2}? The \mark{not} covers only the second half.
qed/level.fo-atoms.tasks.fo-atoms-1.say: Ann is a parent of Bo, yet Bo does not like Ann.
qed/level.fo-atoms.tasks.fo-atoms-2.hint: “Either … or …” has no “not” in it: at least one of the two holds, so it is \mark{or}.
qed/level.fo-atoms.tasks.fo-atoms-2.say: Socrates is either a bird or human.
qed/level.fo-atoms.tasks.fo-atoms-3.hint: “Only if A, B” says: if B holds, A must hold. The condition is the second half.
qed/level.fo-atoms.tasks.fo-atoms-3.say: Ann likes Bo only if Bo is human.
qed/level.fo-atoms.title: Translating a sentence
qed/level.fo-nested.intro.0.t: A quantifier may hold another. Each has its own variable and reaches over everything after it: in \(\forall x\). … \(\exists y\). …, x and y each stand for their own thing. A variable some quantifier covers is a <wiki-ref to="qed/bound"></wiki-ref>; one no quantifier covers is a <wiki-ref to="qed/free"></wiki-ref>, and then the sentence does not say whom it means.
qed/level.fo-nested.tasks.fo-nested-1.br: Use the cards to build a formula for this sentence.
qed/level.fo-nested.tasks.fo-nested-1.hi: Outside, every x; inside, some y: the thing x likes takes another variable.
qed/level.fo-nested.tasks.fo-nested-2.br: Use the cards to build a formula for this sentence.
qed/level.fo-nested.tasks.fo-nested-2.hi: For every x, if x is human, then some y is a parent of x.
qed/level.fo-nested.tasks.fo-nested-3.br: Someone else translated the first sentence too. Build a world where their formula and yours differ in truth.
qed/level.fo-nested.tasks.fo-nested-3.hi: Think of it as a game: the opponent picks for \mark{forall}, you pick for \mark{exists}. In the first, the opponent picks x first, then you pick y; in the second you pick y first, then the opponent picks x.
qed/level.fo-nested.title: One inside another
qed/level.fo-some.intro.0.t: A new symbol, \mark{exists}, reads “there exists”: \(\exists x.\, P(x)\) says at least one thing x in the world satisfies P.
qed/level.fo-some.intro.1.t: First build a sentence as a formula; when it is wrong, the checker may show a small world where it and the target differ. Then someone else has translated the sentence too, and it is your turn to show with a world that they got it wrong.
qed/level.fo-some.tasks.fo-some-1.brief: Use the cards to build a formula for this sentence.
qed/level.fo-some.tasks.fo-some-1.hint.0: “Some bird flies”: there is a thing x that is a bird and flies.
qed/level.fo-some.tasks.fo-some-1.hint.1: Writing “\(x\; \text{is a bird}\to x\; \text{flies}\)” is made true by anything at all that is not a bird.
qed/level.fo-some.tasks.fo-some-2.brief: You built this sentence as a formula; this is someone else’s. Build a world where the two differ in truth.
qed/level.fo-some.tasks.fo-some-2.hint.0: What if the world holds no bird at all?
In propositional logic, whether a sentence is true depends on the row of the truth table. In first-order logic it depends on the world: how many things there are, what each is and how they relate.

Above are your translation and someone else’s. To show theirs is wrong, build a world where the two differ: choose below how many things there are, then tap what holds of each. A run marks above whether each translation is true in this world.
qed/level.fo-some.title: There exists \mark{exists}
qed/level.g-always.after: At least one conditional is true in every case, so the output column is all true. A sentence like this is a <wiki-ref to="qed/tautology"></wiki-ref>. Your circuit is now available as an Always True gate.
qed/level.g-always.intro.0.t: An If–then gate has a direction. If you join the two directions with Or, which rows can come out false?
qed/level.g-always.tasks.g-always-1.brie: Wire a circuit to find the truth value of “‘if it rains, the ground is wet’ or ‘if the ground is wet, it rains’” on every row.
qed/level.g-always.tasks.g-always-1.hint: Wire “it rains” and “the ground is wet” into the two If–then gates in opposite orders.
qed/level.g-always.title: Build an Always True gate
qed/level.g-and.intro.0.t: The new part , written \mark{and}, outputs true only when both inputs are true.
qed/level.g-and.tasks.g-and.brief: Wire a board that works out the value of “it rains and it is not windy” on every row.
qed/level.g-and.tasks.g-and.hint.0: Two things must hold at once: “it rains” and “it is not windy”.
qed/level.g-and.title: Rain, but no wind
qed/level.g-iff.after: When both directions hold, the inputs have matching truth values. This is <wiki-ref to="qed/equivalence"></wiki-ref>, written \mark{iff}. The circuit you built is now available as the “Equivalent” gate.
qed/level.g-iff.intro.0.t: Or required at least one direction to hold. This time, use And to require both directions and see what happens to the output.

qed/level.h-and-make.intro.0.t: <level-ref to="qed/decl-and"></level-ref> brought “and” into the kernel by a declaration. Another way declares nothing and uses the \mark{implies} and quantifier already there: “A and B” is “for every sentence R, if R follows from A and B, then R”, written \mark{forall}R. \((A\to (B\to R))\to R\).
qed/level.h-and-make.intro.1.t: This \mark{forall} ranges not over things but over sentences. The same two parts handle it: take the upper-case name R in the <part-ref to="part:qed/allI"></part-ref>, and inside it R is any sentence at all; in <part-ref to="part:qed/allE"></part-ref> choose not a thing but a sentence, to put in for R.

Inside, the goal is an “if … then …”: assume “\(A\to (B\to R)\)” and Apply twice.

qed/level.h-eq-refl.after: The reflexivity a declaration gives is, under the definition, a conclusion proved.

qed/level.h-eq-refl.intro.1.t: This \mark{forall} ranges over properties: P(x) is a sentence about x. The <part-ref to="part:qed/allI"></part-ref> takes the upper-case P. By this definition, the Morning Star = the Morning Star is this level’s goal.

qed/level.p-exAnd.tasks.p-exAnd-2.brief: The reasoning is written as a lemma. Build a counterexample: every premise holds and the goal fails.
qed/level.p-exAnd.tasks.p-exAnd-2.hint.0: The two \(\exists s\) may point at two different things.
qed/level.p-exAnd.tasks.p-exAnd-2.say: There is a bird, and something flies, so some bird flies.

qed/level.p-only.brief: Use the cards to build a formula for this sentence.
qed/level.p-only.tasks.p-only-1.hint.0: “Only birds fly”: whatever flies is a bird. Which side is the condition?
qed/level.p-only.tasks.p-only-2.hint.0: The outermost part is \mark{not}, over the whole of “every bird flies”.
qed/level.p-only.title: “Only” and “none”
qed/level.p-split.tasks.p-split-1.brief: Use the cards to build a formula for this sentence.
qed/level.p-split.tasks.p-split-1.hint.0: The premise is an “if … then …” with a \mark{forall} sentence on each side; the whole reasoning is another “if … then …”.
qed/level.p-split.tasks.p-split-1.say: If everything is a bird, then everything flies; so every bird flies.
qed/level.p-split.tasks.p-split-2.brief: The reasoning is written as a lemma. Build a counterexample: every premise holds and the goal fails.
qed/level.p-split.tasks.p-split-2.hint.0: The premise’s condition, “everything is a bird”, fails as soon as one thing is not a bird.
qed/level.p-split.tasks.p-split-2.say: If everything is a bird, then everything flies; so every bird flies.
qed/level.p-split.title: Splitting \mark{forall}
qed/level.peirce.after: This is Peirce’s law. Added to a language of \mark{implies} alone, it gives classical logic.
qed/level.peirce.intro.0.t: This sentence has nothing but \mark{implies}. It looks strange, yet it is true on every row.
qed/level.peirce.tasks.peirce.hint.0: Rain or no rain: take both sides.
qed/level.peirce.tasks.peirce.hint.1: On the side where it does not rain, find a way to get “\(\text{it rains}\to \text{the ground is wet}\)”.
qed/level.peirce.title: Peirce’s law
qed/level.pl-anc.intro.0.t: An ancestor is a parent, or a parent’s ancestor: the rule uses itself.
qed/level.pl-anc.tasks.pl-anc.brief: Design a proof assistant that finds every answer to each question.
qed/level.pl-anc.tasks.pl-anc.hint.0: As many generations, so long is the proof.
qed/level.pl-anc.title: Any number of generations (Legacy)
qed/level.pl-grand.after: This is Prolog: a program is a set of rules, and a question is a goal with ?-letters to prove.
qed/level.pl-grand.intro.0.t: In <level-ref to="qed/q-grand"></level-ref>, “grandparent” was written as a query. This time it is a rule: \mark{open-bracket}?x is a parent of ?y; ?y is a parent of ?z\mark{close-bracket} \mark{entails} ?x is a grandparent of ?z. The family tree’s facts are the goal’s givens.
qed/level.pl-grand.intro.1.t: The question itself holds a ?-letter: “?w is a grandparent of Cy”. Who ?w is in each way of proving it is an answer.
qed/level.pl-grand.tasks.pl-grand.brief: Design a proof assistant that finds every answer to each question.
qed/level.pl-grand.tasks.pl-grand.hint.1: Every way of fitting is an answer.
qed/level.pl-grand.title: Who is a grandparent (Legacy)
qed/level.pl-order.after: This is known as left recursion.
qed/level.pl-order.intro.0.t: This time the rule for more generations is written the other way round: first an ancestor ?y of ?x, then whether ?y is a parent of ?z. The meaning is the same.
qed/level.pl-order.tasks.pl-order.brief: Design a proof assistant that finds every answer to each question.
qed/level.pl-order.tasks.pl-order.hint.0: After “counting up” backwards, the first goal is an “ancestor” again.
qed/level.pl-order.title: Ask which first (Legacy)
qed/level.q-allAnd.tasks.q-allAnd.hint.0: Two for-any boxes, each proving one half, then join them.
qed/level.q-allAnd.title: \mark{forall} over both sides
qed/level.q-allE.intro.0.t: A new part, <part-ref to="part:qed/allE"></part-ref>: wire in a “\(\forall x\). …”, choose a thing on the part, and out comes the sentence with x replaced by it.
qed/level.q-allE.tasks.q-allE.hint.0: What holds for every x holds for Ann: on the part, put Ann in for x.
qed/level.q-allE.title: Take one
qed/level.q-allI.after: “Take any a …, so it holds for all x”: the commonest phrase in mathematical proofs means just this box.
qed/level.q-allI.intro.0.t: In <level-ref to="qed/m-counter"></level-ref>, one world showed that something does not follow. To show a sentence holds in every world, the worlds cannot all be checked: it is back to the proof board and its rules.
qed/level.q-allI.intro.1.t: The new for-any box takes an arbitrary object inside the box and names it on the part, for example a. A statement proved about a inside becomes a statement about every object outside. a must not appear in any open assumption. From here on, objects are named a, b or c, while x, y and z are reserved for quantifiers.
qed/level.q-allI.tasks.q-allI.hint.0: Inside the box, prove the sentence with a in place of x.
qed/level.q-allI.tasks.q-allI.hint.1: Inside the box take any thing, call it a, and prove “\(a\; \text{is human}\to a\; \text{is human}\)”; holding for any one at all, outside it is “for all x”.
qed/level.q-allI.title: For any
qed/level.q-ancestor.tasks.q-ancestor.hi: Three \(\forall s\), taken one at a time: x is Ann, y is Bo, z is Cy.
qed/level.q-ancestor.title: An ancestor’s ancestor
qed/level.q-bigger.tasks.q-bigger.hint.0: Take any a; the example of something bigger is a+1.
qed/level.q-bigger.title: Always a bigger one
qed/level.q-capture.after: So the quantifier’s variable is renamed before substituting; the prover’s <part-ref to="part:qed/allE"></part-ref> does this by itself.
qed/level.q-capture.intro.0.t: <part-ref to="part:qed/allE"></part-ref> puts a thing in for x. If what goes in is the variable y and x sits inside an “\(\exists y\)”, that y is caught by the quantifier (<wiki-ref to="qed/capture"></wiki-ref>), and the meaning changes completely: putting y in for x in “everything likes something” seems to give “something likes itself”.
qed/level.q-capture.tasks.q-capture.brie: Here is a lemma someone wrote for the reasoning above. Build a counterexample: every premise holds and the goal fails.
qed/level.q-capture.tasks.q-capture.hint: Two things that like each other and not themselves.
qed/level.q-capture.tasks.q-capture.say: Everything likes something, so something likes itself.
qed/level.q-capture.title: No clashing names
qed/level.q-children.intro.0.t: A sentence with one x left free is a <wiki-ref to="qed/query"></wiki-ref>: the things of a world that make it true when put in for x are the answer. At its core, SQL, the language of databases, is first-order logic like this.
qed/level.q-children.intro.1.t: There are two families here. One query must be right in both, so remembering names will not do.
qed/level.q-children.tasks.q-children.br: Build a sentence with x in it that picks out exactly Ann’s children in each family.
qed/level.q-children.tasks.q-children.sa: x is a child of Ann.
qed/level.q-children.title: Who are Ann’s children
qed/level.q-dm.intro.0.t: “Nobody is drinking” and “everyone is not drinking” say the same. \mark{exists} is like a long “or” and \mark{forall} a long “and”, so <wiki-ref to="qed/demorgan"></wiki-ref> hold for quantifiers too.
qed/level.q-dm.intro.1.t: Once all four directions are proved, <part-ref to="lemma:qed/dm"></part-ref> gains four shapes.
qed/level.q-dm.tasks.q-dm-1.hint.0: Take any a; the goal is “\(\lnot a\) is drinking”.
qed/level.q-dm.tasks.q-dm-1.hint.1: Suppose a is drinking: then a is just the kind of example the given denies.
qed/level.q-dm.tasks.q-dm-2.hint.0: The goal is a negation: suppose someone is drinking.
qed/level.q-dm.tasks.q-dm-2.hint.1: Take that person out; the given holds of them too.
qed/level.q-dm.tasks.q-dm-3.hint.1: Take out the one who is not drinking: they are among “everyone” too.
qed/level.q-dm.tasks.q-dm-4.hint.0: The given names nobody to point to. Try proof by contradiction.
qed/level.q-dm.tasks.q-dm-4.hint.1: Assume “\(\lnot \exists x.\, \lnot x\) is drinking”, and see whether everyone drinking follows.
qed/level.q-dm.title: De Morgan for quantifiers
qed/level.q-eq.intro.0.t: The ancients took the bright star of dawn and the one of dusk for two; later they learned both are Venus. Two names for one thing are written =: .
qed/level.q-eq.intro.1.t: The equality declared in <level-ref to="qed/decl-eq"></level-ref> brought two parts: <part-ref to="part:qed/rewrite"></part-ref> takes s = t and a sentence about s, boxes each s on the part, and replaces the ticked ones by t; <part-ref to="part:qed/refl"></part-ref> gives t = t at once.
qed/level.q-eq.tasks.q-eq.hint.0: Once both wires are in, the part boxes each “the Morning Star”: tick a box and that one becomes “the Evening Star”.
qed/level.q-eq.title: The Morning Star is the Evening Star
qed/level.q-exE.after: “There is one; call it a”: mathematical proofs say this often too.
qed/level.q-exE.intro.0.t: <part-ref to="part:qed/exE"></part-ref> uses an existential statement: connect “\(\exists x\). …” and name the existing object a on the part. Inside the box, you may assume that it satisfies the condition. The name a is temporary: it must not appear in the conclusion outside the box or in other open assumptions.
qed/level.q-exE.tasks.q-exE.hint.0: Inside the box, name the thing a, split, and use it as the example.
qed/level.q-exE.title: Take the one there is
qed/level.q-exI.intro.0.t: <part-ref to="part:qed/exI"></part-ref> uses the introduction rule written in <level-ref to="qed/decl-ex"></level-ref>: an object satisfying a condition shows that such an object exists. Connect a statement about the object; if several existential statements follow, choose the conclusion on the part.
qed/level.q-exI.tasks.q-exI.hint.0: Split out “Ann is mortal” and wire it into <part-ref to="part:qed/exI"></part-ref>.
qed/level.q-exI.title: An example
qed/level.q-grand.tasks.q-grand.brief: Build a sentence with x in it that picks out exactly the grandparents in each family.
qed/level.q-grand.tasks.q-grand.hint.0: x is a parent of y, and y of z. Who are y and z? Some, that is all.
qed/level.q-grand.tasks.q-grand.say: x is a grandparent of someone.
qed/level.q-grand.title: Who are grandparents
qed/level.q-move.intro.0.t: Is “whoever is late, the teacher is cross” the same as “if anyone is late, the teacher is cross”?
qed/level.q-move.tasks.q-move-1.hint.0: Assume someone is late, take them out, and take them from the given.
qed/level.q-move.tasks.q-move-2.hint.0: Take any a and assume they are late: they are the “someone”.
qed/level.q-move.title: Moving a quantifier out
qed/level.q-none.tasks.q-none.brief: Build a sentence with x in it that picks out exactly those with no children in each family.
qed/level.q-none.tasks.q-none.hint.0: What is “x has a child”? Put a \mark{not} in front.
qed/level.q-none.title: Who has no children
qed/level.q-rename.tasks.q-rename.hint.0: Take any a, then take a out of the given.
qed/level.q-rename.title: Another name
qed/level.q-school.tasks.q-school.brief: Build a sentence with x in it that picks out exactly those who have children, all of whom go to school.
qed/level.q-school.tasks.q-school.hint.0: Join two things with \mark{and}: “has children” with \mark{exists}, “all children at school” with \mark{forall}.
qed/level.q-school.tasks.q-school.hint.1: With only “all children at school”, those with no children are picked too: for them it holds with nothing to check, a <wiki-ref to="qed/vacuous"></wiki-ref>.
qed/level.q-school.tasks.q-school.say: x has children, and all of x’s children go to school.
qed/level.q-school.title: Parents whose children all go to school
qed/level.q-swap.after: When a proof will not come, trying for a countermodel is often faster than pushing on.
qed/level.q-swap.tasks.q-swap-1.brief: Here is a lemma someone wrote for the reasoning above. Build a counterexample: every premise holds and the goal fails.
qed/level.q-swap.tasks.q-swap-1.say: Everything is liked by something, so something likes everything.
qed/level.q-swap.tasks.q-swap-2.hint.0: From the outside in: the goal is a \mark{forall} outermost.
qed/level.q-swap.tasks.q-swap-2.hint.1: Take any b; take out the one who likes everything and call them a; take b from what holds of a, then use a as the example.
qed/level.q-swap.title: Swapping quantifiers
qed/level.q-sym.tasks.q-sym.brief: Given “the Morning Star = the Evening Star”, prove “the Evening Star = the Morning Star”.
qed/level.q-sym.tasks.q-sym.hint.0: Reflexivity gives “the Morning Star = the Morning Star”.
qed/level.q-sym.tasks.q-sym.hint.1: Replace only its left Morning Star.
qed/level.q-sym.title: Equal both ways
qed/level.q-trans.tasks.q-trans.brief: Given “the Morning Star = Venus” and “Venus = the Evening Star”, prove “the Morning Star = the Evening Star”.
qed/level.q-trans.title: Equal all along
qed/level.q-witness.tasks.q-witness.brie: Here is a lemma someone wrote for the reasoning above. Build a counterexample: every premise holds and the goal fails.
qed/level.q-witness.tasks.q-witness.hint: Two things: one is Socrates, the other a bird.
qed/level.q-witness.tasks.q-witness.say: There is a bird, so Socrates is a bird.
qed/level.q-witness.title: A borrowed name stays
qed/level.r-allI.intro.0.t: <part-ref to="part:qed/allI"></part-ref> used backwards, \mark{open-bracket}\mark{meta-all}x. ?P(x)\mark{close-bracket} \mark{entails} \(\forall x.\, ?P\)(x): the unifier finds ?P, and the new goal is \mark{meta-all}a. ?P(a). \mark{meta-all} is the rules’ own “for all”, ruling over goals rather than sentences: a is any thing at all, and the goal must hold of it.
qed/level.r-allI.tasks.r-allI.brief: Design a proof assistant that proves every goal.
qed/level.r-allI.tasks.r-allI.hint.0: With the \mark{forall} gone, what remains is the familiar splitting and joining.
qed/level.r-allI.title: For-any box, backwards (Legacy)
qed/level.r-assumption.intro.0.t: Use the assumption box backwards and one “if” comes off the goal. Its condition becomes a given. Sometimes the goal that remains is already one of those givens.
qed/level.r-assumption.intro.1.t: Connect the <part-ref to="part:logic/assumption"></part-ref> card to <part-ref to="part:qed/rule"></part-ref>. If the goal matches a current given, it is proved. The card reads Γ, \(A\vdash A\), where Γ stands for the other givens.
qed/level.r-assumption.tasks.r-assumptio: Design a proof assistant that proves every goal.
With every “if” peeled off, where is the goal that is left?
qed/level.r-assumption.title: Among the givens (Legacy)
qed/level.r-both.intro.0.t: So far the ?-letters have all been on the left. But both sentences being fitted may hold them, and then an equation like “\(\text{it rains}\doteq ?B\)” appears, its ?-letter on the right, where the parts so far do not look. A new part, “Orient”, turns it into ?B \mark{dot-equals} it rains.
qed/level.r-both.tasks.r-both.brief: Design a proof assistant that solves each set of equations to the end, or says “failed” when they do not fit.
qed/level.r-both.tasks.r-both.hint.0: Turn round any equation with its ?-letter on the right.
qed/level.r-both.title: ? on both sides
qed/level.r-cases.intro.0.t: <part-ref to="lemma:qed/erule"></part-ref> takes apart more than “and”: any elimination rule can be chosen on it. Case analysis as a rule is \mark{open-bracket}\(?A\lor ?B\); \mark{open-bracket}?A\mark{close-bracket} \mark{entails} ?C; \mark{open-bracket}?B\mark{close-bracket} \mark{entails} ?C\mark{close-bracket} \mark{entails} ?C.
qed/level.r-cases.tasks.r-cases.brief: Design a proof assistant that proves every goal.
qed/level.r-cases.tasks.r-cases.hint.1: In each case, which side of the goal is among the givens?
qed/level.r-cases.title: Case by case (Legacy)
qed/level.r-clash.intro.0.t: A rule need not fit a goal. Join concludes an “and”; against an “or”, nothing put in for ?A and ?B makes them fit. A new part, “Conflict”, finds an equation with no ?-letter on either side and sides of different shapes, and declares failure. When using rules, failure means trying another rule.
qed/level.r-clash.tasks.r-clash.brief: Design a proof assistant that solves what can be fitted to the end, and says “failed” of what cannot.
qed/level.r-clash.tasks.r-clash.hint.0: Split first, then look for an equation whose sides differ in shape.
qed/level.r-clash.title: They do not fit
qed/level.r-deep.intro.0.t: How many levels must be split depends on the rule and the goal, and is not known beforehand: however many Decompose parts are wired, a deeper equation will come.
qed/level.r-deep.intro.1.t: The <part-ref to="part:qed/repeat"></part-ref> works on equations too: the parts inside do one round, the next round splits what this one gave, until nothing changes or it fails, and it gives the last round.
qed/level.r-deep.tasks.r-deep.brief: Design a proof assistant that splits until each equation has a single ?-letter on its left, however many levels it takes.
qed/level.r-deep.tasks.r-deep.hint.0: One Decompose in the frame; the frame does the rest.
qed/level.r-deep.title: All the way down
qed/level.r-delete.intro.0.t: A rule’s conclusion is not all ?-letters: some places hold fixed sentences, and there the goal must be exactly the same. Split, such a place becomes “it is windy \mark{dot-equals} it is windy”, which says nothing. A new part, “Delete”, removes such equations.
qed/level.r-delete.intro.1.t: \(\lnot A\) in the prover is \(A\to \bot\), and splits as such.
qed/level.r-delete.tasks.r-delete.brief: Design a proof assistant that solves each set of equations to the end, leaving only equations for ?-letters.
qed/level.r-delete.tasks.r-delete.hint.0: Split first, then look at what is left.
qed/level.r-delete.title: Same on both sides
qed/level.r-dist.after: A row of parts like this is a proof script, one part to a line.
qed/level.r-dist.intro.0.t: In <level-ref to="qed/dist"></level-ref> this sentence took several boxes on the proof board. This time, reason back from the goal.
qed/level.r-dist.tasks.r-dist.brief: Design a proof assistant that proves every goal.
qed/level.r-dist.tasks.r-dist.hint.0: First take apart every given that comes apart.
qed/level.r-dist.tasks.r-dist.hint.1: Then split into two cases, and in each choose a side of the “or”.
qed/level.r-dist.title: Distribute (Legacy)
qed/level.r-drule.after: Reasoning on from a given like this is <wiki-ref to="qed/forward"></wiki-ref>.
qed/level.r-drule.intro.0.t: <part-ref to="part:qed/allE"></part-ref> as a rule is \mark{open-bracket}\(\forall x.\, ?P\)(x)\mark{close-bracket} \mark{entails} ?P(?t). Backwards, its conclusion ?P(?t) must fit “Socrates is mortal”, but ?P is followed by ?t, not by a bound variable. Is ?P “x is mortal” with ?t Socrates, or is ?P just “Socrates is mortal” with ?t anything? There is more than one solution, the unifier does not guess, and the part does not fit.
qed/level.r-drule.intro.1.t: On the proof board there was no going backwards: was wired after the “for all” given, and what it gave wired on. Getting a sentence on the way and then using it is, as a rule, Have: \mark{open-bracket}?A; \mark{open-bracket}?A\mark{close-bracket} \mark{entails} ?C\mark{close-bracket} \mark{entails} ?C. Used backwards it adds a goal ?A, and the ?A proved joins the next goal’s givens. comes in at the board’s input Rules; the proof assistant you design becomes a new part, “Forward”, and that input is its port Rules.
qed/level.r-drule.tasks.r-drule.brief: Design a proof assistant that takes one from the “for all” given and adds it to the givens, turning each goal into the one wanted.
qed/level.r-drule.tasks.r-drule.hint.0: Have used backwards leaves a bare ?A as the first goal.
qed/level.r-drule.tasks.r-drule.hint.1: ?A is settled from the “for all” given: <part-ref to="lemma:qed/erule"></part-ref> with <part-ref to="part:qed/allE"></part-ref>.
qed/level.r-drule.title: One step forward (Legacy)
qed/level.r-elim.intro.0.t: The rules used so far all look at the goal: the conclusion fits it, the premises become new goals. Split as a rule is \mark{open-bracket}\(?A\land ?B\); \mark{open-bracket}?A; ?B\mark{close-bracket} \mark{entails} ?C\mark{close-bracket} \mark{entails} ?C: its conclusion ?C fits any goal, but its first premise \(?A\land ?B\) cannot be read off the goal, and becomes a goal made of ?-letters.
qed/level.r-elim.intro.1.t: The rules come in at the board’s input Rules; the proof assistant you design becomes a new part, <part-ref to="lemma:qed/erule"></part-ref>, and that input is its port Rules.
qed/level.r-elim.tasks.r-elim.brief: Design a proof assistant that takes the “and” given apart, turning each goal into the one wanted.
qed/level.r-elim.tasks.r-elim.hint.0: What can settle a goal made of ?-letters?
qed/level.r-elim.tasks.r-elim.hint.1: After the first backward step, try closing the goal with the <part-ref to="part:logic/assumption"></part-ref> card.
qed/level.r-elim.title: A rule, then a given (Legacy)
qed/level.r-exE.intro.0.t: <part-ref to="part:qed/exE"></part-ref> as a rule is \mark{open-bracket}\(\exists x.\, ?P\)(x); \mark{meta-all}x. \mark{open-bracket}?P(x)\mark{close-bracket} \mark{entails} ?C\mark{close-bracket} \mark{entails} ?C. It is an elimination rule too: its first premise fits a “there is”, and the \mark{meta-all}x in front of the second gives the new goal a thing a, with a given about it.
qed/level.r-exE.tasks.r-exE.brief: Design a proof assistant that proves every goal.
qed/level.r-exE.tasks.r-exE.hint.0: The given contradicts itself, about the thing it says there is.
qed/level.r-exE.tasks.r-exE.hint.1: <part-ref to="lemma:qed/erule"></part-ref> with <part-ref to="part:qed/exE"></part-ref>, on the “there is” given.
qed/level.r-exE.title: Taking out, backwards (Legacy)
qed/level.r-exI.intro.0.t: <part-ref to="part:qed/exI"></part-ref> as a rule is \mark{open-bracket}?P(?t)\mark{close-bracket} \mark{entails} \(\exists x.\, ?P\)(x). ?t is a metavariable for a thing: used backwards, the example cannot be read off the goal, so ?t is left open. In <level-ref to="qed/q-exI"></level-ref>, with several “there is” sentences, you chose on the part which to conclude; with a rule used backwards, the goal says so itself.
qed/level.r-exI.tasks.r-exI.brief: Design a proof assistant that proves every goal.
qed/level.r-exI.tasks.r-exI.hint.0: Who the example is, leave to a given.
qed/level.r-exI.title: Generalise, backwards (Legacy)
qed/level.r-false.intro.0.t: The goal has nothing to do with the givens, yet among the givens is a pair that contradict each other.
qed/level.r-false.tasks.r-false.brief: Design a proof assistant that proves every goal.
qed/level.r-false.tasks.r-false.hint.0: Going backwards, what should the goal become first?
qed/level.r-false.tasks.r-false.hint.1: Apply as an elimination rule: which given does it fit?
qed/level.r-false.title: Givens that contradict (Legacy)
qed/level.r-frule.intro.0.t: Going forward does not take the given away: the “for all” sentence is still there after one use, and can be used again, for another thing.
qed/level.r-frule.tasks.r-frule.brief: Design a proof assistant that proves every goal.
qed/level.r-frule.tasks.r-frule.hint.0: Is one use of the “for all” given enough?
qed/level.r-frule.title: The same given twice (Legacy)
qed/level.r-lemma.intro.0.t: A lemma you proved is itself a rule: <part-ref to="lemma:qed/chain"></part-ref> is \mark{open-bracket}\(?A\to ?B\); \(?B\to ?C\)\mark{close-bracket} \mark{entails} \(?A\to ?C\). It can be used backwards just like the kernel’s rules, and the part offers it too.
qed/level.r-lemma.tasks.r-lemma-1.brief: Design a proof assistant that proves every goal with <part-ref to="lemma:qed/chain"></part-ref>.
qed/level.r-lemma.tasks.r-lemma-1.hint.0: The middle sentence of <part-ref to="lemma:qed/chain"></part-ref> cannot be read off the goal.
qed/level.r-lemma.tasks.r-lemma-2.brief: Now prove every goal with <part-ref to="lemma:qed/swap"></part-ref>.
qed/level.r-lemma.tasks.r-lemma-3.brief: Now prove every goal with <part-ref to="lemma:qed/merge"></part-ref>.
qed/level.r-lemma.tasks.r-lemma-3.hint.0: Once <part-ref to="lemma:qed/merge"></part-ref>’s conclusion fits the goal, what is left to prove?
qed/level.r-lemma.title: Lemmas are rules too (Legacy)
qed/level.r-match.intro.0.t: <part-ref to="part:qed/rule"></part-ref> has been fitting a rule’s conclusion to the goal for you, working out which sentences ?A and ?B stand for. Often the goal already says what a card needs. This section takes it apart to see how it works that out.
qed/level.r-match.intro.1.t: A rule can be written with blanks: Join is \mark{open-bracket}?A; ?B\mark{close-bracket} \mark{entails} \(?A\land ?B\), the premises in brackets, the conclusion after \mark{entails}. ?A and ?B are <wiki-ref to="qed/metavariable"></wiki-ref>s. The notation is <wiki-ref to="qed/isabelle"></wiki-ref>’s; <wiki-ref to="qed/lean"></wiki-ref> has metavariables too.
qed/level.r-match.intro.2.t: To use a rule on a goal, its conclusion must first fit the goal: solve \(?A\land ?B\) \mark{dot-equals} it rains \mark{and} it is windy for ?A and ?B. This is <wiki-ref to="qed/unification"></wiki-ref>. A new part, “Decompose”, splits an equation whose sides share a shape into equations between corresponding parts.
qed/level.r-match.tasks.r-match.brief: Design a proof assistant that fits a rule’s conclusion to a goal, splitting until each equation has a single ?-letter on its left.
qed/level.r-match.tasks.r-match.hint.0: One Decompose splits one level. The third test has two.
qed/level.r-match.title: Fitting a rule
qed/level.r-meta.intro.0.t: Apply as a rule is \mark{open-bracket}\(?A\to ?B\); ?A\mark{close-bracket} \mark{entails} ?B. Its conclusion ?B fits the goal “the ground is wet”, but ?A cannot be read off the goal, and stays as it is in both new goals. Whatever settles ?A later settles it in both.
qed/level.r-meta.tasks.r-meta.brief: Design a proof assistant that proves every goal.
qed/level.r-meta.tasks.r-meta.hint.0: Use Apply backwards. Leave ?A open for a given to settle.
qed/level.r-meta.title: An ?A not settled yet (Legacy)
qed/level.r-occurs.after: Many unifiers leave the occurs check out for speed, Prolog among them by default; the price is that something false may be “proved”.
qed/level.r-occurs.intro.0.t: \(?A\doteq ?A\) \mark{implies} the ground is wet: ?A must equal a sentence longer than itself. Put in once, the right side gains another ?A, and it never ends: there is no solution. None of the parts so far can do anything with it; the repeat frame goes round once, nothing changes, and it stops. A new part, “Occurs check”, finds \(?A\doteq t\) with ?A inside t, and declares failure.
qed/level.r-occurs.tasks.r-occurs.brief: Design a proof assistant that solves each set of equations to the end, or says “failed” when there is no solution.
qed/level.r-occurs.tasks.r-occurs.hint.0: When the frame stops, are the equations left really solved?
qed/level.r-occurs.title: It never ends
qed/level.r-order.intro.0.t: Someone is human and likes Ann, so someone likes Ann and is human.
qed/level.r-order.tasks.r-order.brief: Design a proof assistant that proves every goal.
qed/level.r-order.tasks.r-order.hint.0: What ?t may become depends on when it was left.
qed/level.r-order.title: Take it out first (Legacy)
qed/level.r-pattern.after: When a metavariable is followed only by distinct bound variables, the solution is unique: a <wiki-ref to="qed/pattern"></wiki-ref> (Miller’s patterns).
qed/level.r-pattern.intro.0.t: In the quantifier rules a metavariable is followed by variables: <part-ref to="part:qed/allI"></part-ref> is \mark{open-bracket}\mark{meta-all}x. ?P(x)\mark{close-bracket} \mark{entails} \(\forall x.\, ?P\)(x). ?P is not a sentence but “a sentence about x”. Solving \(\forall x.\, ?P\)(x) \mark{dot-equals} \(\forall x.\, x\) is human \mark{implies} x is mortal must give ?P \mark{dot-equals} fun x => x is human \mark{implies} x is mortal: ?P is a function with x as its parameter.
qed/level.r-pattern.intro.1.t: When two “for all” are split, both bodies get the same variable, and the equation is marked \mark{meta-all}x: x is bound by a quantifier. ?A may not take x out with it, so \(\forall x.\, ?A\doteq \forall x.\, x\) is human has no solution (the occurs check checks this too); ?P(x) may, being about x in the first place. A new part, “Pattern unification”: when ?P is followed by distinct \mark{meta-all} variables, it solves ?P.
qed/level.r-pattern.tasks.r-pattern.brie: Design a proof assistant that solves each set of equations to the end, or says “failed” when they do not fit or have no solution.
qed/level.r-pattern.tasks.r-pattern.hint: Let the unifier do what it can, and pass an equation like ?P(x) that is left to the new part.
Once ?P is solved, there may be more unifying to do.
qed/level.r-pattern.title: Pattern unification
qed/level.r-patterns.intro.0.t: ?P(x, y) is a sentence about x and y. Two “for all” split one after the other mark the equation \mark{meta-all}x y; ?P followed by two distinct bound variables is still a pattern.
qed/level.r-patterns.tasks.r-patterns.br: Design a proof assistant that solves each set of equations to the end, or says “failed” when they do not fit or have no solution.
qed/level.r-patterns.tasks.r-patterns.hi: However many variables follow ?P, the function found has that many parameters, in the order they follow ?P.
qed/level.r-patterns.title: Several variables
qed/level.r-rule.intro.0.t: On the proof board a proof is wired downwards from the givens. A proof assistant works the other way, from the goal back: <wiki-ref to="qed/backward"></wiki-ref>. A new part, <part-ref to="part:qed/rule"></part-ref>: wire a rule into its port “R”; it fits the first goal to the rule’s conclusion and replaces that goal with the rule’s premises, one new goal for each. Every proof-board part is, on this board, a part that gives its rule, and several rule parts can be chained into one list.
qed/level.r-rule.intro.1.t: Recall the assumption box rule “\(\llbracket \llbracket ?A\rrbracket \Longrightarrow ?B\rrbracket \Longrightarrow ?A\to ?B\)”. Its conclusion matches an “if” goal. Used backwards, it replaces that goal with “assume ?A and prove ?B”. The wires carry a <wiki-ref to="qed/proof-state"></wiki-ref>, the goals that remain to be proved.
qed/level.r-rule.tasks.r-rule.brief: Design a proof assistant that turns each goal into the one wanted.
qed/level.r-rule.tasks.r-rule.hint.0: The three goals are all “if … then …”. Which of the kernel’s rules makes an “if … then …”?
qed/level.r-rule.title: Rules backwards (Legacy)
qed/level.r-subgoals.intro.0.t: Join has two premises: used backwards, it turns one goal into two, in a row. A part always works on the first goal; when it is proved, the next moves up.
qed/level.r-subgoals.tasks.r-subgoals.br: Design a proof assistant that proves every goal.
qed/level.r-subgoals.tasks.r-subgoals.hi: Are the two halves of the “and” each among the givens?
qed/level.r-subgoals.title: One goal becomes several (Legacy)
qed/level.r-twice.intro.0.t: <part-ref to="lemma:qed/merge"></part-ref>’s premise is \(?A\to (?A\to ?B)\): ?A occurs twice, and both places must be the same sentence. Split, it gives two equations about ?A. A new part, “Eliminate”, finds \(?A\doteq t\) and puts t for ?A in the other equations.
qed/level.r-twice.tasks.r-twice.brief: Design a proof assistant that solves each set of equations to the end, or says “failed” when they do not fit.
qed/level.r-twice.tasks.r-twice.hint.0: Once ?A is known, replace it everywhere else, and see whether the rest fits.
qed/level.r-twice.title: The same ?A twice
qed/level.r-unifier.after: What the unifier finds is the <wiki-ref to="qed/mgu"></wiki-ref>: it settles only what must be settled.
qed/level.r-unifier.intro.0.t: All six kinds of part are in hand: Decompose, Delete, Conflict, Eliminate, Orient, Occurs check. This time any of them may be needed, how often and when depending on the equations. The proof assistant you design becomes a new part, “Unifier”.
qed/level.r-unifier.tasks.r-unifier.brie: Design a proof assistant that solves any set of equations to the end, however many levels and substitutions it takes, or says “failed” when they do not fit or have no solution.
qed/level.r-unifier.tasks.r-unifier.hint: Every kind of part belongs in the repeat frame.
qed/level.r-unifier.title: Six parts, one frame
qed/level.raa.after: The rules without double-negation elimination are <wiki-ref to="qed/intuitionistic"></wiki-ref>; with it, <wiki-ref to="qed/classical"></wiki-ref>. In classical propositional logic, every sentence true on every row has a proof.
qed/level.raa.intro.0.t: In <level-ref to="qed/c-wall"></level-ref>, auto could not prove “\(\text{it rains}\lor \lnot \text{it rains}\)”, an instance of <wiki-ref to="qed/lem"></wiki-ref>. First a weaker sentence: “\(\lnot \lnot (\text{it rains}\lor \lnot \text{it rains})\)”, that denying it is a contradiction.
qed/level.raa.tasks.raa-1.hint.0: The goal is a negation; neither side of the “or” has to be proved.
qed/level.raa.tasks.raa-1.hint.1: Assume “\(\lnot (\text{it rains}\lor \lnot \text{it rains})\)”; that assumption is used twice.
qed/level.raa.tasks.raa-2.hint.0: The proof you just made already gives “\(\lnot \lnot (\text{it rains}\lor \lnot \text{it rains})\)”.
qed/level.raa.tasks.raa-2.hint.1: Wire <part-ref to="part:qed/raa"></part-ref> after the outermost assumption box.
qed/level.raa.tasks.raa-2.intro.0.t: From \(\lnot \lnot A\), infer A: this is double-negation elimination. The rules so far cannot derive it; it can only come into the kernel as an , .
qed/level.raa.title: It holds or it does not
qed/level.read-rules.after: The components box now shows the rules your proof parts give. The premises tell you what to wire in, and the conclusion tells you what comes out. Apply and the assumption box belong to the kernel. Chain gets its rule from a proof you built. Next, give “and” rules of its own.
qed/level.read-rules.intro.0: You can write out what a proof-board part does as a <wiki-ref to="qed/rule"></wiki-ref>: “\mark{open-bracket}premises\mark{close-bracket} \mark{entails} conclusion”. The left side tells you what to wire in. The right side tells you what follows. ?A and ?B can stand for any sentences, and each occurrence of the same placeholder stands for the same sentence.
qed/level.read-rules.intro.1: The rule for <part-ref to="part:qed/mp"></part-ref> is “\(\llbracket ?A\to ?B;?A\rrbracket \Longrightarrow ?B\)”. The rule for the <part-ref to="part:qed/impI"></part-ref> is “\(\llbracket \llbracket ?A\rrbracket \Longrightarrow ?B\rrbracket \Longrightarrow ?A\to ?B\)”. The inner \mark{open-bracket}?A\mark{close-bracket} is available only inside the box. Prove ?B under that assumption, and the box gives you \(?A\to ?B\).
qed/level.read-rules.intro.2: You can also package several proof steps as one part. For example, <part-ref to="lemma:qed/chain"></part-ref> gives “\mark{open-bracket}\(?A\to ?B\); \(?B\to ?C\)\mark{close-bracket} \mark{entails} \(?A\to ?C\)”. Wire these three rules and see what each premise connects to on the board.
qed/level.read-rules.rule-apply.brief: Match the premises of “\(\llbracket ?A\to ?B;?A\rrbracket \Longrightarrow ?B\)” to the two givens, then wire Apply to get the conclusion.
qed/level.read-rules.rule-apply.hint: Find the given with \mark{implies} first. Its condition must match the other given.
qed/level.read-rules.rule-box.brief: Follow the assumption box rule. Assume A inside the box, then use that assumption and the two givens to prove C.
qed/level.read-rules.rule-box.hint: Both givens have condition A. Apply each to A and see what one more application would give you.
qed/level.read-rules.rule-chain.brief: Use Chain to join the two “if” statements, then apply the result to the third given.
qed/level.read-rules.rule-chain.hint: The conclusion of the first given must match the condition of the second.
qed/level.read-rules.title: Read the rule behind a part
qed/level.s-append-both.brief: Use the givens to prove both sides of “and”.
qed/level.s-append-both.hint: Use Join backwards and see how many goals remain.
qed/level.s-append-both.inputs.0.label: Goal
qed/level.s-append-both.intro: Replace “or” with “and”. Splitting the goal now leaves two things to prove. After proving the first, look for the second in the remaining goals.
qed/level.s-append.intro.0.t: To prove “rain or wind”, proving either side is enough. Both alternative rules can open the goal, but a route only works if you can finish it. Keep both routes and see which one matches a given.
qed/level.s-append.tasks.s-append.brief: Design a proof assistant that proves every goal.
qed/level.s-append.tasks.s-append.hint.0: Which side of Add alternative is right need not be decided on the spot any more.
qed/level.s-append.title: One route or two goals (Legacy)
qed/level.s-auto.intro.0.t: You have tried three ways to proceed: match a given, unpack the goal, or use a given to make progress. Wire them as three routes so the assistant has another way to try when a route gets stuck. Your assistant becomes <part-ref to="lemma:qed/auto"></part-ref>.
qed/level.s-auto.tasks.s-auto.brief: Design a proof assistant that proves every goal.
qed/level.s-auto.tasks.s-auto.hint.0: Look at “rain or wind”. Both routes can unpack the goal. Which route can finish the proof?
qed/level.s-auto.tasks.s-auto.hint.1: Wire the possible steps as candidate routes, then let search work out how far to follow each one.
qed/level.s-auto.title: Your own auto (Legacy)
qed/level.s-barbara.after: For over two thousand years the syllogism was nearly all of logic.
qed/level.s-barbara.intro.0.t: Lewis Carroll, author of Alice in Wonderland, was a logician. He made many reasoning puzzles: a few sentences of “all”, “no” and “some”, from which a conclusion must be drawn.
qed/level.s-barbara.intro.1.t: The simplest kind is Aristotle’s syllogism: “all A are B, all B are C, so all A are C”.
qed/level.s-barbara.tasks.s-barbara.hint: Take any a, assume it is a cat, and apply all the way.
qed/level.s-barbara.title: All cats are pets
qed/level.s-carroll.intro.0.t: Carroll’s own puzzle: “babies are illogical”, “whoever can tame a crocodile is respected”, “illogical persons are not respected”. Prove “babies cannot tame crocodiles”.
qed/level.s-carroll.tasks.s-carroll.hint: Take any a and assume it is a baby; to prove “\(\lnot a\) can tame a crocodile”, assume it can, and reach a contradiction.
Baby \mark{implies} illogical \mark{implies} not respected; tames crocodiles \mark{implies} respected: they clash.
qed/level.s-carroll.title: Babies cannot tame crocodiles
qed/level.s-darii.tasks.s-darii.hint.0: Take out the pet that is a cat; it is the example.
qed/level.s-darii.title: Some pets are fluffy
qed/level.s-defer.intro.0.t: When two goals share a placeholder, the goal you prove first can settle it. After Generalise and Join backwards, you still need to prove “?t is human” and “?t likes Ann”. Using the <part-ref to="part:logic/assumption"></part-ref> card on the first goal chooses Cy, but “Cy likes Ann” is not a given.
qed/level.s-defer.intro.1.t: A new part, “Defer”: it moves the first goal to the end.
qed/level.s-defer.tasks.s-defer.brief: Design a proof assistant that proves every goal.
qed/level.s-defer.title: Which goal first (Legacy)
qed/level.s-each.intro.0.t: A part only works on the first goal, so when several goals need the same done, the same parts would be wired several times. A new part, <part-ref to="part:qed/each"></part-ref>: the parts inside run once on each goal, seeing only that goal each time.
qed/level.s-each.tasks.s-each.brief: Design a proof assistant of at most 4 parts that proves every goal.
qed/level.s-each.tasks.s-each.hint.0: The two goals after the join need the same thing done.
qed/level.s-each.title: Every goal (Legacy)
qed/level.s-elim.intro.0.t: Elimination rules look at the givens: a given’s shape says how it can be used. The proof assistant you design becomes a new part, “Use a given”.
qed/level.s-elim.tasks.s-elim.brief: Design a proof assistant that tries every elimination rule on the givens, keeping every fit; when none fits, it fails.
qed/level.s-elim.tasks.s-elim.hint.0: There are six elimination rules: Split, Case analysis, Apply, Explosion, the instance box, choose an instance.
qed/level.s-elim.tasks.s-elim.hint.1: Start each route with the same goal and givens. Bring the results of <part-ref to="lemma:qed/erule"></part-ref> together.
qed/level.s-elim.title: The givens by their shape (Legacy)
qed/level.s-intro.intro.0.t: Until now, the rule for each step was chosen by you after looking at the goals. Introduction rules look at the goal: a goal’s shape says which introduction rule made it. The proof assistant you design becomes a new part, “Goal apart”.
qed/level.s-intro.tasks.s-intro.brief: Design a proof assistant that takes the goal one step apart with every introduction rule that fits, keeping every way; when none fits, it fails.
qed/level.s-intro.tasks.s-intro.hint.0: There are six introduction rules: Join, the assumption box, Add alternative left and right, the for-any box, and Generalise.
qed/level.s-intro.tasks.s-intro.hint.1: Fan the goal out to all six ways of unpacking it. Set the number of routes on <part-ref to="part:qed/append"></part-ref> and connect each result.
qed/level.s-intro.title: The goal by its shape (Legacy)
qed/level.s-lem.intro.0.t: The rule book now holds <part-ref to="part:qed/raa"></part-ref>, as a rule \mark{open-bracket}\(\lnot \lnot ?A\)\mark{close-bracket} \mark{entails} ?A. auto uses only introduction and elimination rules; this rule’s conclusion fits any goal, and in the search it would turn every goal into a “not not”, and again, without end.
qed/level.s-lem.tasks.s-lem.brief: Design a proof assistant that proves the required test goals and reports failure for the designated failure cases.
qed/level.s-lem.tasks.s-lem.hint.1: Before auto, apply a few rules yourself.
qed/level.s-lem.title: auto, after one step by contradiction (Legacy)
qed/level.s-loop.intro.0.t: Ann is older than Bo and Bo older than Cy, so Ann is older than Cy; that Cy is older than Ann follows from nothing. When there is no proof, the proof assistant must still stop and report failure.
qed/level.s-loop.tasks.s-loop.brief: Design a proof assistant that proves the goals that can be proved, and reports failure on the one that cannot.
qed/level.s-loop.tasks.s-loop.hint.0: On the sentence that cannot be proved, where does the search fail to stop?
qed/level.s-loop.tasks.s-loop.hint.1: Each step brings a new ?-letter, so the search cannot tell it is going round.
qed/level.s-loop.title: A search that never stops (Legacy)
qed/level.s-mix.intro.0.t: This time goals nest level within level: some need several “if”s peeled off, some then need Apply used backwards a few times, in a different order each time.
qed/level.s-mix.tasks.s-mix.brief: Design a proof assistant that proves every goal.
qed/level.s-mix.tasks.s-mix.hint.0: What kinds of goal must each round handle?
qed/level.s-mix.tasks.s-mix.hint.1: Fan the same goal out to three routes on each round, then bring their results together.
qed/level.s-mix.title: Try a route at each step (Legacy)
qed/level.s-orelse.after: A tactic can only call the kernel’s rules, so however it is combined it cannot make a false theorem: the design of <wiki-ref to="qed/lcf"></wiki-ref>.
qed/level.s-orelse.intro.0.t: A goal can be worth approaching in two ways. For an “if … then …” goal, take the condition as given. You can also work backwards from the conclusion to see which given helps. Fan the goal out to both routes, then bring their results into <part-ref to="part:qed/append"></part-ref>.
qed/level.s-orelse.tasks.s-orelse.brief: Design a proof assistant that proves every goal.
qed/level.s-orelse.tasks.s-orelse.hint.0: The first step depends on the goal’s shape.
qed/level.s-orelse.tasks.s-orelse.hint.1: Apply backwards can match any goal with its conclusion ?B. Think about which route uses the shape of the goal.
qed/level.s-orelse.title: Or else (Legacy)
qed/level.s-repeat.intro.0.t: So far a proof assistant’s parts have run in a fixed order, fit for goals of one structure; change the nesting and it must be rewired. A program that chooses and combines steps by the proof state is a <wiki-ref to="qed/tactic"></wiki-ref>. Isabelle’s auto and Lean’s simp are tactics.
qed/level.s-repeat.intro.1.t: A new part, the <part-ref to="part:qed/repeat"></part-ref>: on its left the frame opens with the proof state it receives; the parts inside do one round and wire back to “result” on its right; the next round works on this round’s result. So it goes on until the steps inside fail, and it gives the result before the failure.
qed/level.s-repeat.tasks.s-repeat.brief: Design a proof assistant that proves every goal.
qed/level.s-repeat.tasks.s-repeat.hint.0: How many levels of “if … then …” there are is not known beforehand.
qed/level.s-repeat.title: Until it cannot (Legacy)
qed/level.s-results.intro.0.t: In the first case, two givens can help prove “the road is slippery”. Using “if it rains, the road is slippery” leaves “it rains” to prove, and this route gets stuck. The other case offers a similar choice.
qed/level.s-results.intro.1.t: From here on, <part-ref to="part:qed/rule"></part-ref> keeps every matching result. With the <part-ref to="part:logic/assumption"></part-ref> card, each matching given gives a route to continue. Later steps show which routes can finish.
qed/level.s-results.tasks.s-results.brie: Design a proof assistant that proves every goal.
qed/level.s-results.tasks.s-results.hint: The wiring can stay the same. Use Apply backwards once, then use the <part-ref to="part:logic/assumption"></part-ref> card twice.
qed/level.s-results.title: A run of results (Legacy)
qed/level.s-search.after: This is a simple proof assistant: three kinds of step and a backtracking search. Every proof it finds uses only the kernel’s rules, so it is just as trustworthy. There is also what it cannot do: when a given has another “if” inside it (like “\(\text{it rains}\to (\text{it is windy}\to \text{the ground is wet})\)”, which Swap needs), Apply used backwards once does not reach the goal. And it only knows “if … then …”: next the kernel learns new connectives, and the proof assistant will learn to use them too.
qed/level.s-search.intro.0.t: Givens lead into givens: how many times Apply is used backwards, and which given each time, is not known beforehand. The repeat frame follows only the first result, and stops in a dead end.
qed/level.s-search.intro.1.t: A new part, <part-ref to="part:qed/search"></part-ref>: the parts inside take a step, and each result is stepped on again; one path is followed to its end (done, or stuck) before going back for the next. This is <wiki-ref to="qed/dfs"></wiki-ref>. It gives every finished state it finds.
qed/level.s-search.tasks.s-search.brief: Design a proof assistant that proves every goal.
qed/level.s-search.tasks.s-search.hint.1: How many steps is the search’s business.
qed/level.s-search.tasks.s-search.hint.2: If the search does not stop, look for the step that leaves an ?A unsettled, and for what could settle it at once.
qed/level.s-search.title: Search until done (Legacy)
qed/level.s-try.after: A step that may or may not apply is called TRY in tactic languages.
qed/level.s-try.intro.0.t: Some steps may or may not apply: an “and” among the givens should be taken apart, and without one there is nothing to do. But <part-ref to="lemma:qed/erule"></part-ref> fails when it finds no “and”, and the whole proof assistant stops with it.
qed/level.s-try.tasks.s-try.brief: Design a proof assistant that proves every goal.
qed/level.s-try.tasks.s-try.hint.0: Some goals need a given taken apart, some do not.
qed/level.s-try.tasks.s-try.hint.1: Use the result of unpacking the given as the first route. The second route can carry the state through unchanged.
qed/level.s-try.title: A step that may not apply (Legacy)
qed/level.s.intro.0.t: When it rains, if it is windy the ground is wet; when it rains, it is windy. So when it rains, the ground is wet: Apply under the condition “it rains”. This sentence is called <part-ref to="lemma:qed/axS"></part-ref>.
qed/level.s.tasks.s.hint.1: Inside the innermost box, all three assumptions are visible.
qed/level.s.title: Apply under a condition
qed/level.sp-back.intro.0.t: A rewrite rule works only left to right: \(\lnot (A\lor B)\longmapsto \lnot A\land \lnot B\) pushes a negation in, but cannot bring it out.
qed/level.sp-back.tasks.sp-back.brief: Design a proof assistant that makes the two negations in each goal one, outside the brackets.
qed/level.sp-back.tasks.sp-back.hint.0: <part-ref to="lemma:qed/dm"></part-ref> still has shapes you have not used.
qed/level.sp-back.title: Left to right only (Legacy)
qed/level.sp-cnf.after: Automatic provers usually bring a sentence to conjunctive normal form before anything else.
qed/level.sp-cnf.intro.0.t: <wiki-ref to="qed/cnf"></wiki-ref>: negation normal form, with every “or” under the “and”s, a few strings of “or” joined by “and”. Each string of “or” is a <wiki-ref to="qed/clause"></wiki-ref>.
qed/level.sp-cnf.tasks.sp-cnf.brief: Design a proof assistant that transforms each goal into the required form.
qed/level.sp-cnf.tasks.sp-cnf.hint.1: What is left is to bring every “or” under the “and”s.
qed/level.sp-cnf.title: conjunctive normal form (Legacy)
qed/level.sp-dm.intro.0.t: <part-ref to="lemma:qed/dm"></part-ref> has eight shapes, and each can serve as a rewrite rule.
qed/level.sp-dm.tasks.sp-dm-1.brief: Design a proof assistant that pushes the negation in each goal inside the brackets.
qed/level.sp-dm.tasks.sp-dm-1.hint.1: One rewrite rule fits only one shape; to try both, see <part-ref to="part:qed/append"></part-ref>.
qed/level.sp-dm.tasks.sp-dm-2.brief: Design a proof assistant that pushes the negation in each goal past the quantifier.
qed/level.sp-dm.title: Negation pushed in (Legacy)
qed/level.sp-laws.intro.0.t: <part-ref to="lemma:qed/arrow"></part-ref> and <part-ref to="lemma:qed/dist"></part-ref> are equivalences proved both ways too.
qed/level.sp-laws.tasks.sp-laws-1.brief: Design a proof assistant that turns the “if … then …” in each goal into an “or”.
qed/level.sp-laws.tasks.sp-laws-1.hint.0: Look at the two shapes of <part-ref to="lemma:qed/arrow"></part-ref>.
qed/level.sp-laws.tasks.sp-laws-2.brief: Design a proof assistant that distributes the “or” in each goal over the “and”.
qed/level.sp-laws.tasks.sp-laws-2.hint.0: In one goal the “and” is on the right, in the other on the left.
qed/level.sp-laws.tasks.sp-laws-2.hint.1: One rewrite rule fits only one shape; to try both, see <part-ref to="part:qed/append"></part-ref>.
qed/level.sp-laws.title: More rewrite rules (Legacy)
qed/level.sp-nnf.intro.0.t: <wiki-ref to="qed/nnf"></wiki-ref>: no \mark{implies} in the sentence, and every \mark{not} on a smallest sentence.
qed/level.sp-nnf.tasks.sp-nnf.brief: Design a proof assistant that transforms each goal into the required form.
qed/level.sp-nnf.tasks.sp-nnf.hint.1: Then see in front of which connectives and quantifiers a \mark{not} can stand.
qed/level.sp-nnf.title: negation normal form (Legacy)
qed/level.sp-order.intro.0.t: Each time, Simp uses the first rule in the list that fits. The same rules in a different order can give a different sentence.
qed/level.sp-order.tasks.sp-order.brief: Design a proof assistant that brings each goal to its shortest conjunctive normal form.
qed/level.sp-order.tasks.sp-order.hint.0: What happens if you distribute while a negation is still outside?
qed/level.sp-order.title: Which first (Legacy)
qed/level.sp-repeat.intro.0.t: This time the goals hold different numbers of \(\lnot \lnot s\). A rewrite that fits nowhere fails.
qed/level.sp-repeat.tasks.sp-repeat.brie: Design a proof assistant that transforms each goal into the required form.
qed/level.sp-repeat.tasks.sp-repeat.hint: The number of rewrites must depend on the goal.
qed/level.sp-repeat.title: Until nothing fits (Legacy)
qed/level.sp-rw.after: This is the basic move of a <wiki-ref to="qed/simplifier"></wiki-ref>.
qed/level.sp-rw.intro.0.t: To turn the \mark{not}\mark{not}it rains in “it is windy \mark{and} \mark{not}\mark{not}it rains” into it rains, the proof board must take the outer “and” apart, replace the part inside, and put it back together.
qed/level.sp-rw.intro.1.t: Where two sentences are equivalent, one can be swapped for the other right inside a sentence. An equivalence used this way is a <wiki-ref to="qed/rewrite"></wiki-ref>; the new part <part-ref to="part:qed/rw"></part-ref> uses one to change one place in the goal.
qed/level.sp-rw.tasks.sp-rw.brief: Design a proof assistant that takes the \mark{not}\mark{not} out of each goal.
qed/level.sp-rw.tasks.sp-rw.hint.0: Both shapes of <part-ref to="lemma:qed/dneg"></part-ref> can serve as rewrite rules.
qed/level.sp-rw.title: Rewrite (Legacy)
qed/level.sp-simp.after: This is what simp does in Isabelle and Lean too.
qed/level.sp-simp.intro.0.t: Several rewrite rules used together, each time whichever fits, until none fits: this is simplification. The rules come in at the board’s input Rules; the proof assistant you design becomes a new part, , and that input becomes its port Rules.
qed/level.sp-simp.tasks.sp-simp.brief: Design a proof assistant that rewrites each goal with the rules from the input Rules until none of them fits.
qed/level.sp-simp.tasks.sp-simp.hint.0: As in <level-ref to="qed/sp-repeat"></level-ref>, the rewriting goes on until nothing fits.
qed/level.sp-simp.tasks.sp-simp.hint.1: <part-ref to="part:qed/rw"></part-ref> can take a list of rules too, and uses the first that fits.
qed/level.sp-simp.title: Several at once (Legacy)
qed/level.sp-where.intro.0.t: <part-ref to="part:qed/rw"></part-ref> changes one place. When more than one place fits, it changes the first, going outside in and left to right.
qed/level.sp-where.tasks.sp-where.brief: Design a proof assistant that transforms each goal into the required form.
qed/level.sp-where.title: The first place (Legacy)
qed/level.swap.intro.0.t: “On a Saturday, if it rains I rest” and “if it rains, on a Saturday I rest” say the same thing, but the kernel only accepts what is proved.
qed/level.swap.tasks.swap.hint.0: How many \mark{implies}s are in the goal?
qed/level.swap.tasks.swap.hint.1: Inside the innermost box, both conditions are visible.
qed/level.swap.title: Swap the conditions
qed/level.table.after: The forecast is false only if it rains and the ground stays dry. This reading of “if … then …” is called material implication.
qed/level.table.intro.0.t: The forecast says, “If it rains, then the ground is wet.” This statement can be true or false, so it is a proposition.
qed/level.table.intro.1.t: “It rains” and “the ground is wet” can each be true or false, giving four combinations. A <wiki-ref to="qed/truth"></wiki-ref> records one combination per row and shows whether the whole forecast is true in that case.
qed/level.table.intro.2.t: In “if X, then Y”, X is the antecedent and Y is the consequent. Here, “it rains” is the antecedent and “the ground is wet” is the consequent.
qed/level.table.tasks.table.brief: Use the rain and ground conditions in each row to mark “If it rains, then the ground is wet” as true or false.
qed/level.table.tasks.table.hint.0: In which case has the forecast got it wrong?
qed/level.table.tasks.table.hint.1: On the two rows where it does not rain, has the forecast got it wrong?
qed/level.table.title: A promise
qed/level.try-backtracking.after: A rule can apply even when the resulting goal cannot be proved. Join candidates preserves the other route, so Backtracking search can return to it if the first route fails.
qed/level.try-backtracking.intro.0.t: To prove “if it rains, the ground is wet”, you can use an assumption box: add “it rains” to the givens, then try to prove “the ground is wet”. If the full conditional is already a given, you can cite it directly.
qed/level.try-backtracking.intro.1.t: Use Join candidates to send both routes to Backtracking search. Try ① first. If it reaches a dead end, return to the fork and try ②. Switch the run report to the branch tree to see which path finishes the proof.
qed/level.try-backtracking.tasks.try-bac: Use Join candidates inside Backtracking search to combine the two backward cards and finish every proof.
